---
title: "The Modern Era: McVay, Mahomes, Two-High, and the Under-Center Comeback (2017-2025)"
subtitle: "Nine seasons of move and counter-move: the play-action revival, Mahomes, the safeties who stayed deep, the offenses that got bigger to beat them, the quarterback who runs, the coaches who go for it, and the rules that shifted under all of it."
description: "NFL history from 2017 to 2025, and where the game stands entering 2026, told as an arms race: Sean McVay and Kyle Shanahan's 11-personnel, condensed, motion-and-play-action offenses; Patrick Mahomes and Andy Reid's off-script and college-borrowed passing game; the two-high counterrevolution led by Vic Fangio and Brandon Staley and its light boxes; the offensive answer of heavier personnel, the light-box run game and the under-center revival (with nflverse trend charts for two-high coverage, box counts, 11 personnel and under-center snaps); how the slot corner, the star safety, the hybrid linebacker, the move tight end, the edge rusher and the fullback changed; the quarterback run made normal by Lamar Jackson, Jalen Hurts and Josh Allen; fourth-down aggression; the era's rule changes; and Seattle's Super Bowl LX season."
glossary:
  "Two-high counterrevolution": "The NFL's league-wide turn, from about 2019, toward defenses that show two deep safeties before the snap and then either play a two-deep coverage (quarters, Cover 6, Cover 2) or rotate out of that shell at the snap. It answered the play-action and explosive passing offenses of 2017-2020 by taking away the deep ball and the intermediate middle, and it paid for that with lighter boxes against the run. Next Gen Stats measured split-safety coverage on 32.9% of dropbacks in 2018 and 42.0% in 2025. Vic Fangio is the coach most associated with it."
  "Light-box run game": "An offense built to run the ball into boxes of six or fewer defenders, the boxes two-high defenses leave, so that it has as many blockers as the defense has run defenders (or one more, with a second tight end, a fullback or a running quarterback). A steady four- or five-yard run against a light box is the price a two-high defense has agreed to pay; the light-box run game collects it and makes the defense bring a safety down."
  "Under-center revival": "The return, from 2023 to 2025, of the quarterback taking the snap directly behind the center on a larger share of plays (about 27% of plays in 2023 and 34% in 2025, by FTN charting), driven by outside-zone run games, play-action and heavier personnel that want a run and a pass to look identical for as long as possible. Shanahan-tree offenses led it: the 2025 Rams and Seahawks were under center on more than half their plays."
---

```{python}
#| code-summary: "Show the Python (shared drawing helpers for this chapter)"
import os
import re
import logging

import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from matplotlib.patches import FancyArrowPatch, Rectangle, FancyBboxPatch
from matplotlib.lines import Line2D

from gridiron import Play, Player, offense, routes as r, show_animation, style, draw_marker
import gridiron.play as _gp

# The throws in this chapter (deep overs and posts off play-action) are driven, not floated: about 26 yd/s.
_gp.BALL_SPEED = 26.0

logging.getLogger("matplotlib.font_manager").setLevel(logging.ERROR)
style.apply()
PDF = os.environ.get("RTG_FORMAT", "").lower() in ("pdf", "typst", "print")
FIELD_W = 160 / 3
HALF = FIELD_W / 2              # 26.7 yards from the middle of the field to either sideline
TE_RING = style.LINE_TO_GAIN    # gold rings for tight ends and fullbacks, as in Personnel Groupings


def D(key, pos, d, w, label=None):
    """A defender at (d, w): d yards past the line of scrimmage, w yards to the offense's right."""
    return Player(key, pos, "def", d, w, label=label)


def O(key, pos, d, w, label=None):
    return Player(key, pos, "off", d, w, label=label)


def line5():
    """The five offensive linemen, unlabelled except the center."""
    return [p for p in offense("singleback") if p.key in ("LT", "LG", "C", "RG", "RT")]


def no_numbers(ax):
    """Remove the painted yard-line numbers (they sit where wide receivers and corners stand)."""
    for t in list(ax.texts):
        if t.get_alpha() == 0.55:
            t.remove()


def ruler(fld, play, fs=6.5, side="left"):
    """Depth labels (yards past the line of scrimmage) down one edge of the window."""
    ax = fld.ax
    x_edge = FIELD_W - fld.y1 + 0.35 if side == "left" else FIELD_W - fld.y0 - 0.35
    for d in range(5, 41, 5):
        y = play.los + d
        if fld.x0 + 0.8 <= y <= fld.x1 - 0.8:
            ax.text(x_edge, y, f"{d}" + (" yd" if d == 5 else ""), fontsize=fs, color=style.INK_2,
                    ha=side, va="center", zorder=12,
                    bbox=dict(boxstyle="round,pad=0.12", fc=style.SURFACE, ec="none", alpha=0.85))


def pointer(fld, play, text, text_at, to, ha="center", fs=7.0):
    """A labelled arrow from a text box to a spot on the field (both in (d, w) yards)."""
    tx, ty = fld.xy(*play.to_abs(*text_at))
    px, py = fld.xy(*play.to_abs(*to))
    fld.ax.annotate(text, xy=(px, py), xytext=(tx, ty), ha=ha, va="center", fontsize=fs, color=style.INK,
                    zorder=12, arrowprops=dict(arrowstyle="-|>", color=style.INK_2, lw=0.9, shrinkB=6),
                    bbox=dict(boxstyle="round,pad=0.25", fc=style.SURFACE, ec=style.BASELINE, lw=0.6))


def say(fld, play, text, at, fs=7.0, color=None, ha="center", weight="normal"):
    """Plain on-field text at (d, w), on a light patch so lines underneath don't cut it."""
    x, y = fld.xy(*play.to_abs(*at))
    fld.ax.text(x, y, text, ha=ha, va="center", fontsize=fs, color=color or style.INK, zorder=12,
                fontweight=weight, bbox=dict(boxstyle="round,pad=0.2", fc=style.SURFACE, ec="none", alpha=0.95))


def box_outline(fld, play, w=(-8.0, 8.0), d=(0.0, 7.0)):
    """A dashed rectangle around 'the box': tackle box plus a tight end on each side, out to ~7 yards."""
    x0, y0 = fld.xy(*play.to_abs(d[0], w[0]))
    x1, y1 = fld.xy(*play.to_abs(d[1], w[1]))
    fld.ax.add_patch(Rectangle((min(x0, x1), min(y0, y1)), abs(x1 - x0), abs(y1 - y0), fill=False,
                               ec=style.INK_2, lw=0.9, ls=(0, (4, 3)), zorder=2))


def trim(ax):
    """Drop text labels whose anchor lies outside the drawn window (players cropped out of view)."""
    x0, x1 = sorted(ax.get_xlim())
    y0, y1 = sorted(ax.get_ylim())
    for t in list(ax.texts):
        x, y = t.get_position()
        if t.get_transform() == ax.transData and not (x0 <= x <= x1 and y0 <= y <= y1):
            t.remove()


# ---------------------------------------------------------------- moments of a play, for print
def snapshot(play, t, ax=None, lateral=(-HALF, HALF), window=(-9.0, 28.0), width_in=6.5, notes=(),
             show_ruler=False):
    """Everyone where he is at time t, with faint trails of where he has been and the ball's flight."""
    pos = {k: play.position(k, t) for k in play.players}
    moved = [pl.moved(d=float(pos[k][0]), w=float(pos[k][1])) for k, pl in play.players.items()]
    q = Play([m for m in moved if m.side == "off"], [m for m in moved if m.side == "def"],
             los=play.los, ball_y=play.ball_y, to_go=play.to_go)
    q.highlights = dict(play.highlights)
    fld = q.draw(ax=ax, lateral=lateral, window=window, width_in=width_in, title=False)
    ax, ppy = fld.ax, fld.pts_per_yard()
    no_numbers(ax)
    if show_ruler:
        ruler(fld, play, fs=5.5)
    P = lambda d, w: fld.xy(*play.to_abs(d, w))  # noqa: E731
    start = play._compile()[1]
    for k, pl in play.players.items():
        if pl.side == "off" and pl.pos not in ("WR", "TE", "RB", "QB", "FB"):
            continue
        pts = np.array([play.position(k, tt) for tt in np.linspace(start, t, 30)])
        if np.ptp(pts[:, 0]) + np.ptp(pts[:, 1]) < 0.3:
            continue
        xs, ys = P(pts[:, 0], pts[:, 1])
        if pl.side == "off":
            ax.plot(xs, ys, color=style.OFFENSE, lw=1.0, alpha=0.45, zorder=3)
        else:
            ax.plot(xs, ys, color=style.DEFENSE, lw=1.3, ls=(0, (3, 2)), zorder=3)
    bx, by = P(*play.ball_position(t))
    for kind, _, t_rel in play.ball_events:
        if kind == "pass" and t > t_rel:
            sx, sy = P(*play.ball_position(t_rel))
            ax.add_patch(FancyArrowPatch((float(sx), float(sy)), (float(bx), float(by)), arrowstyle="-|>",
                                         mutation_scale=8, color=style.BALL, lw=1.4, ls=(0, (2, 1.5)), zorder=9))
    passes = [t_rel for kind, _, t_rel in play.ball_events if kind == "pass"]
    if not passes or t > passes[0]:
        draw_marker(ax, float(bx), float(by), "ball", "", ppy)
    for text, at in notes:
        say(fld, play, text, at, fs=6.3)
    trim(ax)
    return fld


def strip(play, times, labels, lateral=(-HALF, HALF), window=(-9.0, 28.0), notes_at=None, width_in=6.5, ncols=2,
          extras=None):
    """The print version of an animation: one panel per chosen moment."""
    n = len(times)
    nrows = int(np.ceil(n / ncols))
    pw = width_in / ncols
    h = nrows * (pw * (window[1] - window[0]) / abs(lateral[1] - lateral[0]) + 0.32)
    fig, axes = plt.subplots(nrows, ncols, figsize=(width_in, h), squeeze=False)
    for ax in axes.flat[n:]:
        ax.axis("off")
    for i, (ax, t, lab) in enumerate(zip(axes.flat, times, labels)):
        fld = snapshot(play, t, ax=ax, lateral=lateral, window=window, notes=(notes_at or {}).get(i, ()),
                       show_ruler=(i == 0))
        if extras and i in extras:
            extras[i](fld)
        ax.set_title(lab, fontsize=8.5, color=style.INK, loc="left")
    fig.tight_layout(h_pad=0.6, w_pad=0.4)
    h = [Line2D([], [], color=style.DEFENSE, lw=1.3, ls=(0, (3, 2)), label="Defender's path so far"),
         Line2D([], [], color=style.OFFENSE, lw=1.0, alpha=0.6, label="Offense's path so far"),
         Line2D([], [], color=style.BALL, lw=1.4, ls=(0, (2, 1.5)), label="The ball")]
    fig.legend(handles=h, loc="upper center", bbox_to_anchor=(0.5, 0.0), ncol=3, fontsize=7.5, frameon=False)
    return fig


def catch_time(play, t_from):
    """When the first pass arrives at its receiver (for the last panel of a strip)."""
    _, spot = play.pass_target_spot()
    return next(t for t in np.arange(t_from, 6.0, 0.02) if np.linalg.norm(play.ball_position(t) - spot) < 0.3)
```

February 8, 2026, Super Bowl LX at Levi's Stadium. The Seattle Seahawks beat the New England Patriots
29-13, and their running back, Kenneth Walker III, carried 27 times for 135 yards and was named the
game's MVP. Look at how Seattle got there and the season reads like a list of everything the NFL had
supposedly left behind. On offense, the Seahawks took the snap with the quarterback **under center**,
right behind the center, on more than half their plays, second-most in the league, and played with
fewer than three wide receivers on more than half of them. On defense, they kept two safeties deep on
about half of opponents' dropbacks and still sacked Drake Maye six times in the Super Bowl.[^sblx] Nine
seasons earlier, the most copied offense in football had three wide receivers on the field for almost
every snap, and the defenses it faced usually had one deep safety and eight players crowded near the
line. Nearly every piece of that 2017 picture had flipped by 2025. None of it was nostalgia. Each change
was an answer to the change before it, and this chapter follows the chain, from Sean McVay's first
season in Los Angeles to the morning after Seattle's title, and shows you how to see each link on a
Sunday.

**You'll be able to…**

- Explain what Sean McVay and Kyle Shanahan built in 2017 (one personnel group, tight splits, motion,
  and play-action off the outside zone) and why it tore up the single-high defenses of the day.
- Explain what Patrick Mahomes and Andy Reid added: a passing game borrowed from college and a
  quarterback whose best plays happened after the design broke down.
- Explain the **two-high counterrevolution**, read its trend line, and say what it cost defenses;
  then explain the offensive answer (the **light-box run game**, heavier personnel, and the
  **under-center revival**) by counting blockers and defenders on a diagram.
- Name the positions that changed shape (slot corner, star safety, hybrid linebacker, move tight end,
  edge rusher, fullback) and say which move in the arms race each one answered.
- Explain why the quarterback run became normal this time when it faded after 2012, and why coaches
  started going for it on fourth down, with the numbers behind both.
- List the rule changes of 2017-2026 that matter for strategy and describe where the game stands
  entering the 2026 season.

::: {.callout-note title="You'll need"}
This chapter finishes the history of Part 11 and pulls threads from all over the book. One line each,
with a link if you want to catch up:

- **The previous era** ([Dynasties and Counterpunches](11-04-dynasties-and-counterpunches.qmd)): the
  [move tight end](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-move-tight-end) forced defenses to choose
  [base](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-base-defense) or [nickel](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-nickel)
  before they knew where he'd line up; the [hybrid edge](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-hybrid-edge)
  became a position of its own; the [read-option wave](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-read-option-wave-2012)
  of 2012 came and went; and analysts showed coaches were kicking on fourth down far too often.
- **Two-high and rotation** ([Disguise, Rotation, and Split-Field Coverage](../06-pass-coverage/06-06-disguise-rotation-and-split-field.qmd)):
  a [two-high](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-two-high) shell has two safeties deep before the snap;
  a defense can stay there or rotate one safety down at the snap, so the shell you see isn't always the
  coverage you get.
- **The box** ([A First Look at Defense](../02-personnel-and-formations/02-05-a-first-look-at-defense.qmd)):
  the defenders near the line who can stop a run. A [light box](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-light-box)
  has no more of them than the offense has blockers.
- **Personnel** ([Personnel Groupings](../02-personnel-and-formations/02-01-personnel-groupings.qmd)):
  two digits, backs then tight ends, so [11 personnel](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-11-personnel) is
  one back, one tight end and three receivers, and [12 personnel](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-12-personnel)
  swaps a receiver for a second tight end.
- **Play-action** ([Play-Action, Boots, and Screens](../04-the-passing-game/04-05-play-action-boots-screens.qmd)):
  a pass that starts with a fake handoff, so defenders who read run step the wrong way.
- **EPA** ([Downs, Distance, and Field Position](../01-foundations/01-02-downs-distance-and-field-position.qmd)):
  [expected points added](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-epa), how much a play changed the offense's
  expected score. Positive is good for the offense.
:::

*Reading the diagrams:* offense is blue circles (X, Y, Z, H receivers; Y and U tight ends; F a
fullback; Q quarterback; R running back); defense is outlined squares (E and T ends and tackles; M the
Mike, W the Will and S the Sam linebacker; $ the nickel back; CB corners; FS and SS safeties). Solid arrows are
routes and runs, dashed arrows defenders' movements, tees blocks. Gold rings mark tight ends and
fullbacks, orange rings the defenders to watch, green rings the receiver to watch. A dashed rectangle
marks the box. The dark blue line is the line of scrimmage and the orange line the line to gain.

Three forces push on every row.

- **The passing game kept its head start.** The rules of the previous two decades had tilted the field
  toward throwing, and every offense in this chapter is a way of throwing better: off a run fake, after
  a motion, out of a broken play.
- **Defenses learned to protect the sky.** The single most important defensive change of the era was
  not a new blitz but a decision about where to put the two safeties, and its cost (fewer defenders
  near the line) shaped everything offenses did next.
- **Information got cheap.** Tracking data, public play-by-play models and full-time analysts changed
  how coaches made decisions, most visibly on fourth down.

Now the details, in roughly the order they happened.

## 2017: two young coaches and an old idea

Picture the league McVay walked into. In 2016 the most imitated defense in football was still Pete
Carroll's Seattle [Cover 3](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-cover-3): a single deep safety in the
middle, press-and-bail corners, and a strong safety rolled down near the line as an eighth run defender
(the anatomy is in [The Cover 3 Family](../06-pass-coverage/06-03-cover-3-family.qmd)). Carroll's
former assistants ran it in Jacksonville and Atlanta, and the Falcons reached Super Bowl LI with it.
Offenses, for their part, had mostly moved to the [shotgun](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-shotgun)
(about 64 percent of plays in 2016) and spread the field with three receivers.

The Los Angeles Rams were the league's worst offense that year. They scored 224 points, fewest in the
NFL. In January 2017 they hired Sean McVay, Washington's 30-year-old offensive coordinator, as head
coach, the youngest in the modern NFL. A few weeks later San Francisco hired Kyle Shanahan, the
Atlanta coordinator whose offense had just led the league in scoring. The two had coached together in
Washington from 2010 to 2013 under Shanahan's father, Mike, and both spoke the same football language:
the outside-zone run game and the bootleg passing game that Mike Shanahan and Gary Kubiak had built in
Denver in the 1990s ([Play-Action, Boots, and Screens](../04-the-passing-game/04-05-play-action-boots-screens.qmd)
traces the tree). In McVay's first season the Rams scored 478 points, the most in the league.[^ramsturn]

What did McVay do? Five things, none of them new on its own.

1. **One personnel group.** By 2018 the Rams used [11 personnel](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-11-personnel)
   on about 93 percent of their snaps, against a league median of about 65. A defense learns a lot
   from substitutions; when there aren't any, it learns nothing
   ([Constraint Theory and Sequencing](../08-the-chess-match/08-02-constraint-theory-and-sequencing.qmd)
   calls this the illusion of complexity).
2. **The quarterback under center.** In 2018 Jared Goff took the snap
   [under center](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-under-center) on about 61 percent of plays, the most
   in the league, while the league as a whole did so on about 36 percent.[^rams18uc] Why? With his back to
   the defense and the back running at full speed past him, a run and a run fake look identical for a
   beat longer than they do from the shotgun.
3. **The [outside zone](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-outside-zone) as the base play.** The whole
   line steps sideways, and linebackers have to run with it or get cut off
   ([Zone Running](../03-the-run-game/03-02-zone-running.qmd)).
4. **[Play-action](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-play-action) and boots built to look exactly like
   it.** Goff threw off a run fake on about a third of his dropbacks, more than any quarterback in the
   league.
5. **Tight splits and motion.** The receivers lined up close to the formation (the
   [condensed formation](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-condensed-formation) of
   [Spread and Modern Formations](../02-personnel-and-formations/02-04-spread-and-modern-formations.qmd)),
   close enough to block a linebacker on a run and to release into routes from the same spot on a
   pass, and one of them was often in [motion](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-motion) before the
   snap ([Motion and Shifts as Weapons](../02-personnel-and-formations/02-06-motion-and-shifts.qmd)).

Here is why those five things together beat the defense of the day. A single-high defense gets its
eighth run defender by bringing a safety down, and it asks its linebackers and that safety to attack
the run the moment they see it. Against an offense whose runs and passes looked different, that was a
fine bet. Against an offense whose runs and passes looked the same for the first second, it meant
three defenders stepping forward on every play-action pass, and their steps opened a space on the field
that the McVay offense was built to throw into: the **intermediate middle**, 10 to 18 yards downfield,
behind the linebackers and in front of the deep defenders.

```{python}
#| label: fig-pa-cover3
#| fig-cap: "Play-action against single-high, 2018 style (simulated; an illustration of the idea, not a specific Rams play). Snap: 11 personnel in a condensed set, the quarterback under center; the defense is in Cover 3 with eight in the box, the strong safety (SS) rolled down. +0.9 s: the line and the back show outside zone to the right, and the three run-first defenders (ringed: both linebackers and the strong safety) step toward it, as they must against a real run. The quarterback has turned his back to the defense to fake the handoff and is now booting to his left, away from the fake. +2.6 s: Z, from the right side, has crossed behind the linebackers; on the left, X's vertical route has taken the corner deep and H's flat route has pulled the nickel back ($) wide, and the quarterback, clear of the unblocked end, throws. Last panel: Z catches the deep over about 12 yards downfield near the left numbers, in the hole between the flat and the deep third, with no defender within seven yards."
def pa_cover3():
    off = line5() + [O("QB", "QB", -1.9, 0, "Q"), O("RB", "RB", -7.0, 0.0, "R"), O("Y", "TE", -0.7, 4.8, "Y"),
                     O("Z", "WR", -1.5, 9.0, "Z"), O("X", "WR", -0.7, -10.0, "X"), O("H", "WR", -1.5, -6.6, "H")]
    dfn = [D("WDE", "DE", 1.0, -4.4, "E"), D("WDT", "DT", 1.0, -0.7, "T"), D("SDT", "DT", 1.0, 2.35, "T"),
           D("SDE", "DE", 1.0, 5.6, "E"), D("WILL", "WILL", 4.5, -2.6), D("MIKE", "MIKE", 4.5, 1.6),
           D("SS", "SS", 6.0, 6.8), D("NB", "NB", 4.5, -7.4, "$"), D("LCB", "CB", 6.5, -10.6, "CB"),
           D("RCB", "CB", 6.5, 10.0, "CB"), D("FS", "FS", 13.0, 0.0)]
    p = Play(off, dfn, los=30, to_go=10)
    for k in ("LT", "LG", "C", "RG", "RT"):                   # outside-zone steps to the right
        p.block(k, pts=[(0.3, 1.5)])
    p.block("Y", pts=[(0.4, 1.0)])
    for k in ("WDT", "SDT", "SDE"):
        p.rush(k, pts=[(-0.4, 0.6)], speed=1.5)
    p.path("WDE", [(0.2, -3.2)], absolute=True, speed=2.5)    # the backside end squeezes on the fake...
    p.path("WDE", [(-4.5, -6.2)], absolute=True, speed=4.5, delay=0.3)   # ...then chases the boot
    p.path("RB", [(-5.6, 2.4), (-2.6, 6.8)], absolute=True, speed=6.0)
    p.path("QB", [(-3.2, 1.0)], absolute=True, speed=4.0)                  # reverse out, fake...
    p.path("QB", [(-6.2, -4.0), (-6.4, -6.2)], absolute=True, speed=6.0)  # ...and boot away from it
    p.route("Z", r.path((6.0, -2.0), (11.0, -12.0), (14.0, -22.0)), speed=8.2)
    p.route("X", r.path((8.0, 2.0), (24.0, 3.0)))
    p.route("H", r.path((3.0, 3.0), (4.0, 7.0)), speed=6.5)
    p.pass_to("Z", t=2.6)
    p.path("MIKE", [(3.0, 3.4)], absolute=True, speed=3.2)                 # run-first defenders step up...
    p.path("MIKE", [(8.0, -1.0)], absolute=True, speed=5.0, delay=0.25)    # ...and recover too late
    p.path("WILL", [(3.4, -0.6)], absolute=True, speed=3.2)
    p.path("WILL", [(7.5, -4.0)], absolute=True, speed=5.0, delay=0.25)
    p.path("SS", [(3.4, 5.4)], absolute=True, speed=4.0)
    p.drop("NB", (4.5, -12.5), speed=5.5)                                  # curl-flat player widens with H
    p.drop("LCB", (14.0, -12.5), speed=4.5); p.drop("LCB", (22.0, -12.8), speed=5.5)
    p.drop("RCB", (16.0, 11.0), speed=4.5)
    p.drop("FS", (17.0, -1.0), speed=3.5)
    p.highlight("MIKE", "WILL", "SS", color=style.DEFENSE)
    p.highlight("Z")
    return p


pa = pa_cover3()
PA_T = [0.0, 0.9, 2.6, round(float(catch_time(pa, 2.6)) + 0.04, 2)]
if PDF:
    strip(pa, PA_T, ["Snap · condensed 11, eight in the box", "+0.9 s · three defenders bite on the fake",
                     "+2.6 s · Z crosses behind them: throw", f"+{PA_T[3]:.1f} s · the catch, 12 yards deep"],
          lateral=(-18.0, 18.0), window=(-9.5, 25.5),
          notes_at={1: [("run fake", (-6.4, 7.6))], 3: [("nobody left\nin the hole", (16.2, -6.0))]})
    plt.show()
else:
    show_animation(pa, times=PA_T)
```

Follow the three ringed defenders. None of them does anything wrong. The Mike and Will see the line
step and the back run toward the sideline, and they come up to fill their gaps; the strong safety, the
eighth man the defense brought down for exactly this, attacks the edge. In a Cover 3 defense those three
are also the players who guard the middle of the field against passes. By the time they see the
quarterback pull the ball back and run the other way, they are four or five yards out of position, and
the receiver crossing behind them is running away from all of them. The corner on that side is deep
with the vertical route, the nickel back is wide with the flat route, and nobody is left in the
middle. The same logic killed the Tampa 2 Mike in the last chapter: find the defenders with two jobs
and make them do the wrong one first.

::: {.callout-important title="Why it exists: the McVay-Shanahan offense"}
**What it solves.** A defense reads the offense in a fixed order: personnel, formation, then the first
step of the play. McVay's offense made all three tell the defense the same thing every time (11
personnel, a tight formation, an outside-zone step), so the defense had to defend the run honestly and
was a beat late on everything else. Motion added a last-second problem, because a defense has to
adjust to it and every adjustment leaks information.

**What it costs.** It needs a run game good enough to fear; play-action against a defense that doesn't
respect the run is just a slow dropback with the quarterback's back turned. It asks receivers to block
linebackers and safeties. The long fakes and boots take time, so the quarterback is exposed to the
unblocked backside end, as in the figure. And the sameness is a two-way street: a defense that can make
the run fake *not* matter (by keeping its middle defenders deep no matter what) takes the best part of
the offense away. That is exactly what happened next.
:::

::: {.callout-note title="Film room: Rams 2018 — the high point, and the first answers"}
The 2018 Rams went 13-3, scored 527 points, and reached Super Bowl LIII. On November 19 they beat Kansas
City 54-51 in a Monday night game that seemed like a preview of the league's future
([Early Downs and Field Zones](../10-situational-football/10-01-early-downs-and-field-zones.qmd) has it).
Then the league's two most respected defensive minds got a look at them. On December 9 in Chicago, Vic
Fangio's Bears held the Rams to 6 points and intercepted Goff four times. Eight weeks later, in the Super
Bowl, Bill Belichick's Patriots held them to 3 and won 13-3.[^bears18]

**What to notice:** in both games, watch the Rams' zone runs before you watch their passes. Against the
condensed 11-personnel sets, the Bears lined up six defenders on the line of scrimmage with one
linebacker behind them (a "6-1" front), and the Patriots borrowed the same
six-man front for the Super Bowl. With a defender over every gap, the line's sideways steps found nobody
to cut off: Todd Gurley ran 11 times for 28 yards in Chicago. Without a run to fear, the fake stopped
pulling anyone forward, and the Rams nearly stopped calling it: play-action on 11 of Goff's 48
dropbacks against the Bears, against about 36 percent all season. New England added a surprise of its
own, playing far more zone coverage than it had all year, and Goff, hesitant and under pressure, never
found the rhythm.
Fangio's way of doing that, safeties who stay deep and a front that holds the run without them, is the
seed of the rest of this chapter. Belichick's plan has its own diagram in
[Belichick and Game-Plan Football](../12-case-studies/12-02-belichick-patriots-game-plan.qmd).
:::

Shanahan's 49ers took a slightly different road to the same place. Where McVay lived in 11 personnel,
Shanahan used a fullback, Kyle Juszczyk, and a tight end, George Kittle, who could each block and catch,
so he could show heavy personnel and still throw. His 2019 team went 13-3 and reached Super Bowl LIV. The
case study [The Shanahan Tree](../12-case-studies/12-03-shanahan-wide-zone-tree.qmd) follows that
offense and the coaches it produced, who by 2025 were calling plays all over the league.

## Mahomes, Reid, and the play after the play

The other offensive revolution of 2018 came from Kansas City, and it worked on a different axis. Andy
Reid had been a head coach since 1999, a West Coast offense coach from Mike Holmgren's Green Bay staffs
who had spent two decades building passing games out of short, timed throws and screens. In 2017 the
Chiefs traded up to draft Patrick Mahomes tenth overall out of Texas Tech, where he had played in Kliff
Kingsbury's [Air Raid](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-air-raid), the pass-everything college system
of four- and five-receiver sets and a few concepts practised endlessly. Mahomes sat for almost all of his
rookie season (he started only the final regular-season game), then in 2018, his first as a starter, threw for 5,097 yards and 50 touchdowns and was named MVP. The Chiefs
scored 565 points, the most in the league.[^mahomes18]

Two things made the Reid-Mahomes offense different from McVay's.

**It borrowed from college, openly.** Reid's staffs were known around the league for studying college
film and lifting whole ideas from it: the RPO (a run with a pass option attached, decided by reading one
defender; [RPOs](../04-the-passing-game/04-06-rpos.qmd)), the shovel option, jet motion, and the Air
Raid concepts Mahomes already knew. In 2017, the season before Mahomes started, Reid had already gone
back to Alex Smith's college film at Utah and built RPOs, zone reads and shovel passes into the
Chiefs' offense: "we went back and kind of looked at some of the stuff he had done in college and was
familiar with," he said.[^reidcollege] Where McVay made every play look like one run, Reid made his offense look like many
different college offenses, often in the same game.

**Its best plays were often not the plays that were called.** Mahomes's gift was the
[off-script play](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-off-script-play)
([Quarterback Play](../04-the-passing-game/04-07-quarterback-play.qmd)): the play after the design
breaks down, when the quarterback escapes the rush, keeps his eyes downfield and throws from an angle
no defense practises against, including, once, left-handed. A defense can study a play-caller's
tendencies. It cannot study a scramble.

That combination is why Kansas City matters to this chapter's arms race. McVay's offense punished a
defense that put too many players near the line. Mahomes punished a defense that left any receiver
alone deep, because given an extra second and a broken pocket he would find him. Against both at once,
the natural defensive answer was the same: keep more players back, deep, with everything in front of
them. By 2021, by this book's count from nflverse charting data, defenses played a two-high coverage
against the Chiefs on about 46 percent of labelled dropbacks, the third-highest share against any
offense and well above the league's 38 percent.[^kctwohigh] The Chiefs' answer to that answer was
patience: fewer deep shots, more of the short game Reid had always loved, Travis Kelce underneath, and
Mahomes's legs when the rush came. It worked. From the 2019 season to the 2024 season Kansas City
played in five of six Super Bowls and won three of them.[^chiefssbs]

::: {.callout-note title="Film room: Super Bowl LIV, February 2, 2020 — third-and-15"}
The Chiefs trailed San Francisco 20-10 with 7:13 left in the fourth quarter and faced third-and-15 at
their own 35. Mahomes took a deep drop, held the ball while Tyreek Hill ran a long, deep-breaking route
that the Chiefs called "Jet Chip Wasp," and threw it 44 yards to Hill at the San Francisco 21. Kansas
City scored three touchdowns in the last seven minutes and won 31-20.[^sb54]

**What to notice:** both halves of the offense in one snap. The design is Reid's: a route built to
attack a defense that was playing deep and soft on third-and-long, and a protection (the "chip": a back
bumping the edge rusher on his way out) built to buy time. The time is Mahomes's: he holds the ball past
the moment most quarterbacks would check it down. Defending that offense meant defending both, and
the cheapest way to do it was to put more players deep.
:::

## The two-high counterrevolution

By 2019 defensive coaches had two problems: play-action that pulled their middle defenders forward,
and quarterbacks who punished any single-covered receiver deep. Both problems had the same root. A
single-high defense commits its eighth defender to the run *before the snap*, and modern offenses had
learned to make that commitment cost something on every play.

The answer that swept the league is what this book calls the
[**two-high counterrevolution**](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-two-high-counterrevolution): defenses
that line up with two safeties deep, play a two-deep coverage
([quarters](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-quarters), [Cover 6](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-cover-6),
Cover 2) or rotate out of that shell only at the snap, and accept fewer defenders near the line in
exchange. It is a "counter" revolution because it reverses the previous decade's direction. Seattle's
era had pulled safeties down toward the line; this pushed them back.

Its roots are in college. As [Disguise, Rotation, and Split-Field Coverage](../06-pass-coverage/06-06-disguise-rotation-and-split-field.qmd)
tells it, quarters defenses at Michigan State, TCU and Nick Saban's schools spent the 2000s learning to
play the run with safeties at 10 to 12 yards. In the NFL the coach most associated with it is **Vic
Fangio**, a defensive assistant for more than thirty years, the Bears' coordinator from 2015 to 2018 and,
at 60, a first-time head coach in Denver from 2019. Fangio's defenses kept two safeties deep, played
quarters-based coverages that read the receivers in front of them, and disguised which coverage was
coming until the snap. His protégé **Brandon Staley** took the system to the Rams in 2020, and with Aaron
Donald inside and Jalen Ramsey moving around the secondary, the Rams allowed the fewest points in the
league. Staley was a head coach a year later, and coaches from Fangio's and Staley's staffs (Joe Barry,
Sean Desai, Ejiro Evero, Chris Shula) spread the approach from there.[^fangio] Fangio himself coordinated
the Eagles' defense to a Super Bowl title in the 2024 season.

The idea has three parts.

1. **Keep a lid on the field.** Two deep safeties take away the explosive pass, and because they sit at
   10 to 14 yards reading the receivers in front of them, they also sit right where McVay's crossers and
   Mahomes's deep shots wanted to go. The run fake loses its prize: a safety reading a receiver doesn't
   care what the back is doing.
2. **Let the front hold the run, and fit it late with the safeties.** With both safeties back, the
   [box](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-box) usually has six defenders against six blockers (five
   linemen and a tight end). The defensive line has to win its own fights, and the safeties come
   downhill to make the tackle after the runner is past the line, at five or six yards instead of two.
3. **Don't tell the quarterback.** A two-high shell is the best starting point for disguise, because
   either safety can rotate down at the snap and turn it into a single-high coverage, or neither does
   ([post-snap rotation](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-post-snap-rotation) in 06-06). The quarterback
   who reads "two-high" before the snap may be wrong a second later.

The second part is the bargain, and it deserves a picture.

```{python}
#| label: fig-light-box-run
#| fig-cap: "The bargain, simulated: an inside-zone run against a two-high defense with six in the box (an illustration, not a specific play). Snap: 11 personnel in the shotgun with the tight end attached on the right; the defense has four linemen and two linebackers in the box (dashed rectangle) and both safeties (ringed) at about 12 yards. The offense has six blockers, five linemen and the tight end, so every box defender has a man. +0.6 s: the handoff; the linemen double-team the two defensive tackles and climb to the linebackers. +1.4 s: the back is through the line untouched. +2.2 s: the two safeties arrive from depth and make the tackle about 5 or 6 yards downfield. That is a good run for the offense, and it is exactly the run the defense agreed to give up."
def light_box_run():
    off = line5() + [O("QB", "QB", -5.0, 0, "Q"), O("RB", "RB", -5.0, -1.6, "R"), O("Y", "TE", -0.7, 4.8, "Y"),
                     O("X", "WR", -0.7, -15.0, "X"), O("H", "WR", -1.5, -9.0, "H"), O("Z", "WR", -1.5, 14.0, "Z")]
    dfn = [D("WDE", "DE", 1.0, -4.1, "E"), D("WDT", "DT", 1.0, -0.7, "T"), D("SDT", "DT", 1.0, 2.35, "T"),
           D("SDE", "DE", 1.0, 5.7, "E"), D("WILL", "WILL", 4.5, -2.0), D("MIKE", "MIKE", 4.5, 1.8),
           D("NB", "NB", 5.0, -9.6, "$"), D("LCB", "CB", 7.0, -15.0, "CB"), D("RCB", "CB", 7.0, 14.0, "CB"),
           D("FS", "FS", 12.5, -8.0), D("SS", "SS", 12.5, 8.0)]
    p = Play(off, dfn, los=40, to_go=10)
    p.block("LT", target="WDE")
    p.block("LG", target="WDT"); p.block("C", pts=[(0.5, -0.3)]); p.block("C", target="WILL", delay=0.25)
    p.block("RG", target="SDT"); p.block("RT", pts=[(0.5, 0.0)]); p.block("RT", target="MIKE", delay=0.25)
    p.block("Y", target="SDE")
    p.path("QB", [(-5.0, 0.4), (-5.6, -2.5)], absolute=True, speed=3.0)
    p.run("RB", [(-4.8, 0.3), (-1.2, 1.5), (1.8, 2.2), (5.6, 2.7)], absolute=True, speed=6.2)
    p.handoff("RB", t=0.55)
    p.path("WILL", [(3.6, -0.6)], absolute=True, speed=2.5)
    p.path("MIKE", [(3.8, 2.3)], absolute=True, speed=2.5)
    p.path("FS", [(11.6, -7.0)], absolute=True, speed=2.5)                     # read...
    p.path("FS", [(6.6, 1.6)], absolute=True, speed=6.4, delay=0.05)           # ...then trigger downhill
    p.path("SS", [(11.6, 7.0)], absolute=True, speed=2.5)
    p.path("SS", [(6.5, 3.9)], absolute=True, speed=6.4, delay=0.05)
    p.drop("LCB", (9.0, -15.0), speed=2.5); p.drop("RCB", (9.0, 14.0), speed=2.5)
    p.drop("NB", (5.5, -8.0), speed=2.0)
    p.highlight("FS", "SS", color=style.DEFENSE)
    return p


lb = light_box_run()
LB_T = [0.0, 0.6, 1.4, 2.2]


def _box(fld):
    box_outline(fld, lb, w=(-7.6, 7.6), d=(0.0, 6.6))


if PDF:
    strip(lb, LB_T, ["Snap · six in the box, six blockers", "+0.6 s · handoff; doubles climb",
                     "+1.4 s · through the line", "+2.2 s · safeties tackle at 5-6 yards"],
          lateral=(-17.0, 17.0), window=(-8.5, 16.5), extras={0: _box},
          notes_at={0: [("two-high", (15.0, 0.0))], 3: [("5-6 yards", (2.6, -4.6))]})
    plt.show()
else:
    show_animation(lb, times=LB_T)
```

Five yards on a run looks like a win for the offense, and it is a small one. But think about what the
defense bought with it. In 2025, early-down runs against six or fewer box defenders averaged about 4.6
yards; against seven or more, about 4.1. In expected points, runs against light boxes were still slightly
*negative* on average (about −0.04 EPA per play), just less negative than runs against heavier boxes
(about −0.09).[^lightbox] Meanwhile the thing the defense was protecting against, the 20-yard pass and the
50-yard touchdown, got rarer: quarterbacks threw 20 or more yards downfield on about 10 percent of their
attempts against two-high coverages in 2025, against about 11 percent against single-high ones. A
defense that gives up an extra half-yard per run to take away a few deep balls a game is making a
trade the numbers like, as long as its front can hold.

Here is the whole era in the data.

```{python}
#| code-summary: "Show the Python (the era in numbers: coverage, box counts, personnel and formation, 2016-2025)"
#| output: false
from gridiron.data import nfl, pbp

SEASONS = list(range(2016, 2026))
PB = pbp(SEASONS, columns=["season", "season_type", "game_id", "play_id", "posteam", "play_type", "down",
                           "shotgun", "qb_dropback", "qb_scramble", "epa"])
PB = PB[(PB["season_type"] == "REG") & PB["play_type"].isin(["pass", "run"]) & PB["down"].notna()]
PART = pd.concat([nfl().load_participation([y]).to_pandas()[
    ["nflverse_game_id", "play_id", "offense_personnel", "defenders_in_box", "defense_coverage_type"]]
    for y in SEASONS], ignore_index=True)
M = PB.merge(PART, left_on=["game_id", "play_id"], right_on=["nflverse_game_id", "play_id"])


def count(s, positions):
    """Players at some positions in a personnel string ('1 RB, 1 TE, 3 WR' through 2022; every roster
    position from 2023, e.g. '1 C, 2 G, 1 QB, 1 RB, 2 T, 1 TE, 3 WR')."""
    if not isinstance(s, str):
        return np.nan
    return sum(int(n) for n, pos in re.findall(r"(\d+)\s+([A-Z]+)", s) if pos in positions)


M["rb"] = M["offense_personnel"].map(lambda s: count(s, {"RB", "FB"}))
M["te"] = M["offense_personnel"].map(lambda s: count(s, {"TE"}))
M["wr"] = M["offense_personnel"].map(lambda s: count(s, {"WR"}))
K = M[M["rb"].notna() & M["te"].notna()]

# post-snap coverage on labelled dropbacks (2018 on; no labels in 2016-2017)
CV = M[(M["qb_dropback"] == 1)].copy()
CV["c"] = CV["defense_coverage_type"].astype(str).str.upper()
CV = CV[CV["c"].isin(["COVER_0", "COVER_1", "COVER_2", "2_MAN", "COVER_3", "COVER_4", "COVER_6", "COVER_9"])]
CV["two"] = CV["c"].isin(["COVER_2", "2_MAN", "COVER_4", "COVER_6"])

RUNS = M[(M["play_type"] == "run") & (M["qb_scramble"] == 0) & M["defenders_in_box"].notna()]

TREND = pd.DataFrame({
    "two_high": CV.groupby("season")["two"].mean() * 100,
    "light_box": RUNS.groupby("season")["defenders_in_box"].apply(lambda s: (s <= 6).mean()) * 100,
    "p11": K.groupby("season").apply(lambda g: ((g["rb"] == 1) & (g["te"] == 1)).mean()) * 100,
    "under_center": (1 - PB.groupby("season")["shotgun"].mean()) * 100,
    "lt3wr": K.groupby("season")["wr"].apply(lambda s: (s < 3).mean()) * 100,
}).reindex(SEASONS)
```

```{python}
#| label: fig-era-trends
#| fig-cap: "The arms race in five lines, 2016-2025 (regular seasons; this book's calculation from nflverse play-by-play and participation data). Left, what defenses did: two-high coverages (Cover 2, 2-Man, quarters and Cover 6) as a share of dropbacks with a charted coverage, which starts in 2018 because 2016-2017 have no labels; and the share of designed runs that faced six or fewer defenders in the box. Right, what offenses did: 11 personnel, snaps not in the shotgun (almost all under center; a few pistol), and snaps with fewer than three wide receivers. The dashed line marks a change of data source (Next Gen Stats through 2022, FTN charting from 2023), so read jumps across it with care; Next Gen Stats' own two-high series, which doesn't cross a source change, climbs from 32.9% in 2018 to 42.0% in 2025. Two-high climbs steadily from 2018; light boxes follow; then, in 2025, offenses get heavier and go back under center."
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(6.6, 3.4), sharey=True)
T = TREND
panels = [
    (axes[0], "What defenses did", [("two_high", "Two-high coverage", style.DEFENSE),
                                     ("light_box", "Runs into a light box", style.SERIES[3])]),
    (axes[1], "What offenses did", [("p11", "11 personnel", style.OFFENSE),
                                     ("under_center", "Under center", style.SERIES[2]),
                                     ("lt3wr", "Fewer than 3 WRs", style.SERIES[6])]),
]
for ax, title, series in panels:
    ax.axvline(2022.5, color=style.MUTED, lw=0.9, ls=(0, (4, 3)), zorder=1)
    for col, lab, c in series:
        s = T[col].dropna()
        ax.plot(s.index, s.values, marker="o", ms=3.2, color=c, lw=1.8)
        ax.text(s.index[-1] + 0.25, s.values[-1], f"{s.values[-1]:.0f}%", fontsize=6.8, color=style.INK_2,
                va="center")
    ax.set_title(title, fontsize=9)
    ax.set_xlim(2015.6, 2026.4)
    ax.set_xticks([2016, 2018, 2020, 2022, 2024])
    ax.tick_params(labelsize=7)
    ax.grid(axis="x", visible=False)
    ax.set_ylim(15, 72)
axes[0].set_ylabel("share of plays (%)", fontsize=7.5)
axes[0].text(2022.6, 70, "data source\nchanges", fontsize=6.3, color=style.INK_2, va="top")
# direct labels, placed by hand where each line has room
axes[0].text(2018.1, T.loc[2018, "two_high"] - 4.2, "Two-high coverage", fontsize=6.9, color=style.DEFENSE_DARK)
axes[0].text(2016.0, T.loc[2016, "light_box"] + 3.6, "Runs into a light box\n(6 or fewer in the box)",
             fontsize=6.6, color="#9a6a00", linespacing=1.1)
axes[1].text(2018.7, 67.2, "11 personnel", fontsize=6.9, color=style.OFFENSE_DARK)
axes[1].text(2018.6, 28.6, "Under center", fontsize=6.9, color="#12805a")
axes[1].text(2016.0, 44.0, "Fewer than 3 WRs", fontsize=6.9, color=style.SERIES[6])
fig.tight_layout(w_pad=1.2)
plt.show()
```

Read it left to right, the way the coaches lived it.[^trendcalc]

- **Two-high climbs.** In the nflverse charting, two-high coverages went from about 33 percent of
  dropbacks in 2018 to about 43 percent in 2025. Next Gen Stats, measuring the same thing with
  its own tracking, has 32.9 percent in 2018, 37.8 in 2021, 40.4 in 2024 and a record 42.0 percent in
  2025, when every defense in the league was above 30 percent and quarters alone was 17 percent of
  coverages.[^ngstwohigh]
- **The boxes empty.** Runs against six or fewer defenders went from about 37 percent of designed runs
  in 2018 to more than half in 2024 and 2025. (Part of the jump in 2024 may be how the new charting
  service counts the box; the direction matches every other source.)
- **Offenses keep three receivers out, until they don't.** 11 personnel barely moved from 2016 to 2024,
  around 60 to 64 percent of plays. Then, in 2025, it fell to its lowest share of the decade, and
  snaps with fewer than three receivers jumped to about 42 percent. Shotgun use peaked in 2023 at about
  72 percent of plays, and under-center snaps came back, from about 28 percent of plays in 2023 to
  about 34 percent in 2025.

The left panel is the counterrevolution. The right panel is the counter to the counter, and its last
season is the most interesting season in the chart.

::: {.callout-caution title="Common misconception"}
"Two-high is a soft, prevent-style defense." It looks soft before the snap, with safeties 12 yards deep
and corners off. But the two-high defenses of this era were built to *move*: a quarters safety is the
first run defender to the edge on his side, a rotating safety can arrive as a robber in the middle of
the field at the snap, and the shell is a disguise for single-high coverages and pressures as often as
it is a coverage in itself. The 2020 Rams, 2023 Ravens and 2024 Eagles, three defenses built on
two-high shells and late rotation, each allowed the fewest points or yards in the league. Soft defenses
don't do that. (Notice, too, that a shell is not a coverage: in the charting, Fangio's 2024 Eagles
*played* a two-high coverage after the snap on only about a third of dropbacks, below the league
average, because so many of their two-high looks rotated into single-high ones at the snap.)
:::

## The offense answers: bigger, tighter, and under center

If the defense keeps two safeties deep and six in the box, the offense's first question is simple
arithmetic. How many blockers can it put against those six?

From 11 personnel the answer is six: five linemen and a tight end. Six against six means every
defender is blocked if everyone wins, but nobody is left over to handle a missed block, and the runner
has to make the last defender miss. Now take a receiver off the field and put on a second tight end, or
a fullback. Seven blockers against six. The defense has three choices, and none of them is free:

- **Stay in its nickel, two-high shell** and be outnumbered in the box. The offense runs.
- **Bring a safety down**, at the snap or before it, to get to seven. Now it is single-high again, and
  the offense is back in McVay's world, with play-action against defenders who must respect the run.
- **Substitute bigger players**, a third linebacker or a third safety, to match the heavy personnel.
  Now the offense can spread those bigger players out and throw at the linebacker covering a tight end,
  the [move tight end](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-move-tight-end)'s dilemma from
  [Dynasties and Counterpunches](11-04-dynasties-and-counterpunches.qmd).

That arithmetic is the [**light-box run game**](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-light-box-run-game):
an offense built to run into the boxes two-high defenses leave, with enough blockers that the defense
must either concede the run or give up its shell to stop it. Here are the two eras' pictures side by
side.

```{python}
#| label: fig-two-snaps
#| fig-cap: "Nine seasons apart (illustrative alignments). Left, a 2018-style snap: 11 personnel in a condensed set, the quarterback under center, against a single-high defense with the strong safety (SS) rolled down, eight defenders in the box (dashed rectangle) and one safety deep. Right, a 2025-style snap: 12 personnel (two tight ends, gold rings) under center, against a nickel two-high defense with six in the box and two safeties deep. In 2018 the defense outnumbers the offense's blockers near the line (eight defenders, six blockers) and the offense throws behind them; in 2025 the offense outnumbers the defense (seven blockers, six defenders) and dares it to bring a safety down."
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(6.6, 3.9))
offA = line5() + [O("QB", "QB", -1.9, 0, "Q"), O("RB", "RB", -7.0, 0.0, "R"), O("Y", "TE", -0.7, 4.8, "Y"),
                  O("Z", "WR", -1.5, 9.0, "Z"), O("X", "WR", -0.7, -10.0, "X"), O("H", "WR", -1.5, -6.6, "H")]
dA = [D("WDE", "DE", 1.0, -4.4, "E"), D("WDT", "DT", 1.0, -0.7, "T"), D("SDT", "DT", 1.0, 2.35, "T"),
      D("SDE", "DE", 1.0, 5.6, "E"), D("WILL", "WILL", 4.5, -2.6), D("MIKE", "MIKE", 4.5, 1.6),
      D("SS", "SS", 6.0, 6.8), D("NB", "NB", 4.5, -7.4, "$"), D("LCB", "CB", 6.5, -10.6, "CB"),
      D("RCB", "CB", 6.5, 10.0, "CB"), D("FS", "FS", 13.0, 0.0)]
a = Play(offA, dA, los=35, to_go=10)
a.highlight("Y", color=TE_RING)
fa = a.draw(ax=axes[0], lateral=(-14.5, 14.5), window=(-8.8, 16.8), title=False)
no_numbers(fa.ax)
box_outline(fa, a, w=(-8.3, 8.3), d=(0.0, 7.3))
say(fa, a, "8 in the box", (8.6, -9.6), fs=6.8, color=style.DEFENSE_DARK)
say(fa, a, "one deep safety", (15.1, 0.0), fs=6.8)
say(fa, a, "6 blockers", (-4.0, 9.6), fs=6.8, color=style.OFFENSE_DARK)
axes[0].set_title("2018: 11 personnel vs. one-high", fontsize=9, loc="left", color=style.INK)

offB = line5() + [O("QB", "QB", -1.9, 0, "Q"), O("RB", "RB", -7.0, 0.0, "R"), O("Y", "TE", -0.7, 4.8, "Y"),
                  O("U", "TE", -0.7, -4.8, "U"), O("X", "WR", -1.5, -12.5, "X"), O("Z", "WR", -1.5, 11.5, "Z")]
dB = [D("WDE", "DE", 1.0, -6.0, "E"), D("WDT", "DT", 1.0, -1.2, "T"), D("SDT", "DT", 1.0, 2.35, "T"),
      D("SDE", "DE", 1.0, 6.0, "E"), D("WILL", "WILL", 4.5, -2.0), D("MIKE", "MIKE", 4.5, 2.2),
      D("NB", "NB", 5.5, -9.4, "$"), D("LCB", "CB", 7.0, -12.5, "CB"), D("RCB", "CB", 7.0, 11.5, "CB"),
      D("FS", "FS", 12.5, -7.0), D("SS", "SS", 12.5, 7.0)]
b = Play(offB, dB, los=35, to_go=10)
b.highlight("Y", "U", color=TE_RING)
fb = b.draw(ax=axes[1], lateral=(-14.5, 14.5), window=(-8.8, 16.8), title=False)
no_numbers(fb.ax)
box_outline(fb, b, w=(-8.3, 8.3), d=(0.0, 7.3))
say(fb, b, "6 in the box", (8.6, -2.0), fs=6.8, color=style.DEFENSE_DARK)
say(fb, b, "two deep safeties", (15.1, 0.0), fs=6.8)
say(fb, b, "7 blockers", (-4.0, 9.6), fs=6.8, color=style.OFFENSE_DARK)
axes[1].set_title("2025: 12 personnel vs. two-high", fontsize=9, loc="left", color=style.INK)
fig.tight_layout(w_pad=0.6)
plt.show()
```

Offenses took the second and third answers seriously, and the 2025 numbers in the trend chart are the
result. [12 personnel](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-12-personnel) reached 24 percent of plays,
its highest share in the decade of data, and 13 personnel (three tight ends) 5 percent; Next Gen Stats
counted fewer than three wide receivers on 41.7 percent of plays, the first season at or above 38
percent since it began tracking in 2016. Defenses answered in kind: they played base defense on 29.7
percent of snaps, up from a low of 20.5 percent in 2023.[^heavy] Some offenses went further than others.
The 2025 Rams, McVay's team, the same coach who had lived in 11 personnel in 2018, used three tight ends
on about 31 percent of their snaps. Shanahan's 49ers had a fullback on the field for 37 percent of
theirs.[^team25]

### Why under center?

The trend chart's green line is the other half of the answer, and it is the one most fans notice
first, because it changes what the quarterback looks like before the snap. This book calls it the
[**under-center revival**](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-under-center-revival): the quarterback
taking the snap directly behind the center on about a third of plays in 2025, up from about a quarter
in 2023, with Shanahan-tree offenses leading. The 2025 Rams were under center on 59 percent of their
plays, the Seahawks on 53, and the Bills, Lions, Bears and 49ers between 46 and 50 percent, against a
league average of 34.

Why would an offense give up the shotgun, the alignment that lets the quarterback see the whole
defense and throw quickly? Four reasons, each tied to the two-high defense.

1. **The run gets better.** On an outside-zone or duo run from under center, the back takes the ball
   already running downhill at full speed, aiming wherever the blocks open; from the shotgun he starts
   beside the quarterback and has to run sideways first. Against a light box, the offense wants the run
   to be as good as it can be.
2. **The fake gets better.** From under center the quarterback turns his back to the defense to hand
   off or to fake it, and the linebackers and safeties can't see the ball. From the shotgun the fake is
   in plain view.
3. **The safety has to decide.** This is the big one. In a two-high defense the safeties are the extra
   run defenders: one of them has to come down and fit the run, late, from depth. A run that looks the
   same as play-action for a full second makes that safety guess. If he comes down, the play-action
   pass goes behind him. If he waits, the run gets its five yards.
4. **The pre-snap picture tells the defense less.** In the shotgun, a back offset to one side tells a
   defense something about which way a run can go and who is staying in to block. A back seven yards
   behind a quarterback under center can go anywhere.

The cost is real. A quarterback under center takes longer to set up and sees the defense later; a
dropback from under center is slower than one from the gun; and on obvious passing downs the shotgun
still wins, which is why third-and-long remains a shotgun down for almost every team. The revival is a
first-and-second-down weapon.

```{python}
#| label: fig-pa-two-high
#| fig-cap: "The payoff, simulated: play-action from 12 personnel under center against a two-high (quarters) defense with six in the box (an illustration of the idea, not a specific team's play). Snap: two tight ends attached (gold rings), the quarterback under center; two safeties at 12 yards. +0.9 s: both tight ends block and the back runs the outside-zone fake to the right. To the strong safety (SS, orange ring), reading the tight end in front of him, it is a run, and in a light box he is the man who must fit it, so he comes down hard. +2.0 s: Z has run past the corner's outside leverage and broken to the post, into the space the strong safety just left; the quarterback, finished with his fake and his drop, throws. Last panel: the catch, about 22 yards downfield, with the safety still turning around. Against a light box the run is good enough that the safety has to come; the under-center fake makes the pass look like that run."
def pa_two_high():
    off = line5() + [O("QB", "QB", -1.9, 0, "Q"), O("RB", "RB", -7.0, 0.0, "R"), O("Y", "TE", -0.7, 4.8, "Y"),
                     O("U", "TE", -0.7, -4.8, "U"), O("X", "WR", -1.5, -12.5, "X"), O("Z", "WR", -1.5, 11.5, "Z")]
    dfn = [D("WDE", "DE", 1.0, -6.0, "E"), D("WDT", "DT", 1.0, -1.2, "T"), D("SDT", "DT", 1.0, 2.35, "T"),
           D("SDE", "DE", 1.0, 6.0, "E"), D("WILL", "WILL", 4.5, -2.0), D("MIKE", "MIKE", 4.5, 2.2),
           D("NB", "NB", 5.5, -9.4, "$"), D("LCB", "CB", 7.0, -12.5, "CB"), D("RCB", "CB", 7.0, 11.5, "CB"),
           D("FS", "FS", 12.5, -7.0), D("SS", "SS", 12.5, 7.0)]
    p = Play(off, dfn, los=30, to_go=10)
    for k in ("LT", "LG", "C", "RG", "RT"):
        p.block(k, pts=[(0.3, 1.4)])
    p.block("Y", pts=[(0.5, 1.0)]); p.block("U", pts=[(0.4, 1.2)])
    for k in ("WDT", "SDT", "SDE", "WDE"):
        p.rush(k, pts=[(-0.4, 0.5)], speed=1.5)
    p.path("RB", [(-5.6, 2.4), (-2.4, 6.4)], absolute=True, speed=6.0)
    p.path("QB", [(-3.0, 1.0)], absolute=True, speed=3.6)                  # turn and fake...
    p.path("QB", [(-7.6, 0.4)], absolute=True, speed=4.6)                  # ...then finish the drop
    p.route("Z", r.path((9.0, 0.5), (24.0, -8.0)), speed=7.8)
    p.route("X", r.path((24.0, 0.5)))
    p.pass_to("Z", t=2.0)
    p.path("MIKE", [(2.8, 3.4)], absolute=True, speed=3.0)
    p.path("MIKE", [(7.0, 1.5)], absolute=True, speed=4.5, delay=0.2)
    p.path("WILL", [(3.0, -0.4)], absolute=True, speed=3.0)
    p.path("WILL", [(7.0, -3.0)], absolute=True, speed=4.5, delay=0.2)
    p.path("SS", [(11.6, 6.6)], absolute=True, speed=2.0)                  # reads the tight end: run!
    p.path("SS", [(4.6, 6.0)], absolute=True, speed=6.5)                   # triggers to fit it...
    p.path("SS", [(8.0, 5.0)], absolute=True, speed=4.5, delay=0.15)       # ...and turns back, late
    p.drop("RCB", (9.5, 12.2), speed=2.4); p.drop("RCB", (18.0, 11.5), speed=5.5)   # outside leverage on Z
    p.drop("LCB", (10.0, -12.5), speed=3.0); p.drop("LCB", (20.0, -12.0), speed=5.5)
    p.drop("FS", (16.0, -6.0), speed=3.5)
    p.drop("NB", (6.5, -9.0), speed=2.0)
    p.highlight("Y", "U", color=TE_RING)
    p.highlight("SS", color=style.DEFENSE)
    p.highlight("Z")
    return p


pa2 = pa_two_high()
PA2_T = [0.0, 0.9, 2.0, round(float(catch_time(pa2, 2.0)) + 0.04, 2)]
if PDF:
    strip(pa2, PA2_T, ["Snap · 12 personnel under center, two-high", "+0.9 s · the strong safety fits the 'run'",
                       "+2.0 s · Z breaks behind him: throw", f"+{PA2_T[3]:.1f} s · the catch, 22 yards deep"],
          lateral=(-17.5, 17.5), window=(-9.0, 26.0), width_in=5.9,
          notes_at={1: [("run fake", (-6.2, 9.0))], 3: [("where the\nsafety was", (14.5, 9.0))]})
    plt.show()
else:
    show_animation(pa2, times=PA2_T)
```

Compare this play with the 2018 one. The geometry is the same: a run fake pulls a defender who guards
the middle forward, and the ball goes behind him. What changed is *who* gets pulled. In 2018 it was the
linebackers and a box safety, who were always going to attack the run. In 2025 it is a deep safety, who
is only attacking the run because the box is light and the offense has more blockers than the defense
has bodies. The offense had to earn that by being good enough at running into light boxes that the
safety couldn't wait.

::: {.callout-caution title="Common misconception"}
"The under-center comeback means football is going back to the 1990s." The pictures rhyme, but
almost everything inside them is new. The 1990s offense lined up under center because that was where
quarterbacks stood; the 2025 offense does it to beat a specific defense, and it still runs RPOs, motion
at the snap and spread passing concepts from the same alignment. The 1990s defense played an eighth man
in the box against two tight ends; the 2025 defense keeps two safeties deep against them and fits the
run from 12 yards. Even the fullback is different: the modern one is as likely to run a route as to
lead-block. History doesn't repeat here. It gets folded into the next scheme.
:::

::: {.callout-note title="Film room: Eagles 2024 — both halves of the argument on one roster"}
The 2024 Philadelphia Eagles are the clearest single team to watch for this section, because they played
both sides of it. On defense, Vic Fangio ran his two-high-shell, light-box system and the Eagles
allowed the fewest yards in the league ([Run Fits and Box Math](../05-defensive-fronts-and-run-defense/05-05-run-fits-and-box-math.qmd)
has the film room on how the front held up). On offense, Saquon Barkley ran for 2,005 yards behind one of
the best lines in football, and about 61 percent of his carries came against six or fewer defenders in
the box, where he averaged 5.9 yards. Jalen Hurts's tush push (below) handled the short yardage. The
Eagles beat Kansas City 40-22 in Super Bowl LIX, with a four-man rush that never needed to blitz
Mahomes.[^eagles24]

**What to notice:** on an Eagles run, count the box before the snap. Then watch the opposing safeties: if
the box is light and the run gets to them, they make the tackle at five or six yards, and the Eagles are
happy to keep doing that all afternoon. When a safety starts creeping down to stop it, watch for the
play-action shot behind him.
:::

## Positions mutate

An arms race changes the soldiers as well as the weapons. Over nine seasons, six positions changed
shape, and every change is an answer to something earlier in this chapter. The map below puts them on
one field.

```{python}
#| label: fig-positions
#| fig-cap: "Where the positions changed, 2017-2025 (illustrative alignment). Offense in 21 personnel with a move tight end (Y) split into the slot and a fullback (F) in the backfield (gold rings); defense in nickel with two deep safeties, its edge rushers (E), its hybrid linebacker (W) and its nickel or star (the $) ringed. Each label says what the position became and which move in the arms race made it that way."
off = line5() + [O("QB", "QB", -1.9, 0, "Q"), O("FB", "FB", -4.5, 0.0, "F"), O("RB", "RB", -7.0, 0.0, "R"),
                 O("Y", "TE", -1.5, 8.5, "Y"), O("X", "WR", -0.7, -15.0, "X"), O("Z", "WR", -0.7, 15.5, "Z")]
dfn = [D("WDE", "DE", 1.0, -5.0, "E"), D("WDT", "DT", 1.0, -1.2, "T"), D("SDT", "DT", 1.0, 2.35, "T"),
       D("SDE", "DE", 1.0, 5.0, "E"), D("MIKE", "MIKE", 4.8, -1.2), D("WILL", "WILL", 4.5, 3.6),
       D("NB", "NB", 5.0, 8.8, "$"), D("LCB", "CB", 6.5, -15.0, "CB"), D("RCB", "CB", 6.5, 15.5, "CB"),
       D("FS", "FS", 12.5, -8.0), D("SS", "SS", 12.5, 8.0)]
pm = Play(off, dfn, los=35, to_go=10)
pm.highlight("Y", "FB", color=TE_RING)
pm.highlight("WDE", "SDE", "NB", color=style.DEFENSE)
pm.highlight("WILL", color=style.DEFENSE)
f = pm.draw(lateral=(-HALF + 0.3, HALF - 0.3), window=(-12.5, 22.2), width_in=6.3)
no_numbers(f.ax)
pointer(f, pm, "EDGE: the premium\ndefender. Sacks beat a\npassing game, and an edge\nwho wins alone frees the\nsafeties to stay deep.",
        (16.3, -18.2), (1.6, -5.4), fs=6.4)
pointer(f, pm, "Nickel / star: the slot corner\nbecame the base defense; against\ntwo tight ends, a third safety\n(the big nickel) plays here.",
        (16.9, 15.2), (5.6, 9.2), fs=6.4)
pointer(f, pm, "Hybrid LB/S: a linebacker\nlight enough to cover,\nor a safety playing\nlinebacker.", (16.9, -1.6), (5.2, 3.8), fs=6.4)
pointer(f, pm, "Move TE: blocks in-line, runs\nroutes from the slot, and makes\nthe defense pick its personnel\nbefore it knows where he'll be.",
        (-7.0, 17.6), (-1.9, 8.9), fs=6.4)
pointer(f, pm, "Fullback: a niche revival.\nA seventh blocker against\na light box, and a receiver\nwhen nobody covers him.",
        (-7.0, -12.6), (-4.6, -0.6), fs=6.4)
plt.show()
```

Take them one at a time.

**The slot corner, and the nickel as the base defense.** When offenses went to three receivers on most
snaps, the third receiver needed a third cornerback, the
[slot cornerback](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-slot-cornerback) or nickel back. Through this era
defenses had five or more defensive backs on the field for roughly two-thirds to three-quarters of
snaps (about 66 percent in 2017 and 78 percent in 2023, then back to 69 percent in 2025 as offenses got
heavier).[^dbshare] The nickel back stopped being a substitute and became a starter, and the "base"
4-3 or 3-4 became the package a team played on a minority of snaps
([A First Look at Defense](../02-personnel-and-formations/02-05-a-first-look-at-defense.qmd) charts it).

**The star, and the big nickel.** Then the offenses got heavier again, and a 185-pound slot corner
stuck in the box against two tight ends became a target. The answer was a safety in the nickel spot:
the [big nickel](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-big-nickel), whose fifth defensive back is a
third safety big enough to fit a run and fast enough to cover a tight end. Defenses call him the
"star," and the best of them, such as Kyle Hamilton in Mike Macdonald's Ravens defense or Brian Branch
in Detroit, line up deep, in the slot, on the line and in the box, sometimes in the same series. Seattle
answered the move tight end this way a decade earlier with Kam Chancellor; the two-high era made it
standard.

**The hybrid linebacker and safety.** Linebackers had to cover more and more space: tight ends,
backs in the flat, crossers behind them. Teams drafted lighter, faster linebackers and moved safeties
down to play the position. Not every experiment worked: Isaiah Simmons, drafted eighth overall in 2020
as a "positionless" linebacker-safety, never found a home in Arizona's defense.[^simmons] But the
direction held. In a two-high defense with six in the box, the two linebackers have more ground to cover
against the run *and* the pass than anyone in the old 4-3, and the players who can do both are the ones
who play.

**The move tight end.** The receiving tight end of the last chapter became the centre of offenses:
Travis Kelce in Kansas City, George Kittle in San Francisco, Mark Andrews in Baltimore, and a younger
generation such as Brock Bowers, who set the record for catches by a rookie in 2024.[^bowers] He is the
reason 12 personnel worked as an answer to two-high: one personnel group that can be a seven-blocker run
formation or a spread passing formation, with the defense choosing its players first.

**The edge rusher, the premium defender.** The [edge rusher](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-edge-rusher),
the [hybrid edge](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-hybrid-edge) of the last chapter, became the most
valuable defender in the game, and for a reason this chapter can now state precisely. A two-high defense
needs pressure without blitzing, because every blitzer comes out of the coverage it is trying to keep.
An edge who wins on his own is what lets the safeties stay deep. The market priced it: in 2025, Myles
Garrett, T.J. Watt and Micah Parsons all signed contracts worth about $40 million a year or more, the
richest ever for non-quarterbacks, and Garrett then set the single-season sack record with 23.[^edge]

**The fullback, a niche revival.** The fullback almost disappeared in the spread era. He came back,
in small numbers, in the offenses that wanted a seventh blocker against light boxes: Shanahan's 49ers
(Kyle Juszczyk, signed in 2017 to what was then by far the richest fullback contract in the league),
the Ravens (Patrick Ricard), and the 2025 Seahawks.[^juszczyk] League-wide, two-back personnel stayed
around 7 or 8 percent of plays. The revival is in what he does, not how often he plays: the modern
fullback motions, catches passes and lines up as a tight end, which is why defenses can't just treat
him as a lead blocker and load the box.

## The quarterback runs, and this time it sticks

[Dynasties and Counterpunches](11-04-dynasties-and-counterpunches.qmd) ended the 2012 read-option
wave with a line: the wave receded; the tide came in later. This is the tide.

It came in with **Lamar Jackson**. The Ravens drafted him with the last pick of the first round in 2018,
he took over as the starter midseason, and in 2019 they rebuilt the offense around him under a new
coordinator, Greg Roman, promoted from the 2018 staff: a run
game with a quarterback who was a real runner on every snap, heavy personnel, and option reads from the
[pistol](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-pistol) and the shotgun. In 2019 Jackson ran for 1,206 yards,
then the record for a quarterback, threw 36 touchdown passes, and was the unanimous MVP; the Ravens ran
for 3,296 yards, the most by any team in NFL history.[^lamar19] He won a second MVP in 2023.

Then the others. **Jalen Hurts** led the Eagles to two Super Bowls (the 2022 and 2024 seasons) with
designed runs, scrambles and the [tush push](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-tush-push), the
quarterback sneak with teammates shoving from behind that the Eagles turned into a near-automatic first
down ([Red Zone, Goal Line, and Short Yardage](../10-situational-football/10-03-red-zone-goal-line-and-short-yardage.qmd)
has it). **Josh Allen**, a 6-foot-5 quarterback with a cannon for an arm, ran for double-digit
touchdowns in multiple seasons, won the MVP in 2024 and, by the end of 2025, had more career rushing
touchdowns than any quarterback in history. Jayden Daniels ran for more than 850 yards as a rookie in
2024 and took Washington to the NFC Championship Game.[^allen]

```{python}
#| code-summary: "Show the Python (how much of the running game quarterbacks do, 2006-2025)"
#| output: false
QRB = pbp(range(2006, 2026), columns=["season", "season_type", "play_type", "rusher_player_id", "rushing_yards",
                                      "qb_kneel", "passer_player_id", "pass_attempt"])
QRB = QRB[QRB["season_type"] == "REG"]
_att = QRB[QRB["pass_attempt"] == 1].groupby(["season", "passer_player_id"]).size().rename("n").reset_index()
_QBS = set(map(tuple, _att.loc[_att["n"] >= 150, ["season", "passer_player_id"]].values))
_runs = QRB[(QRB["play_type"] == "run") & (QRB["qb_kneel"] != 1) & QRB["rusher_player_id"].notna()].copy()
_runs["is_qb"] = [(s, rid) in _QBS for s, rid in zip(_runs["season"], _runs["rusher_player_id"])]
QB_SHARE = (_runs[_runs["is_qb"]].groupby("season")["rushing_yards"].sum()
            / _runs.groupby("season")["rushing_yards"].sum() * 100)
_y = _runs[_runs["is_qb"]].groupby(["season", "rusher_player_id"])["rushing_yards"].sum()
QB400 = (_y >= 400).groupby("season").sum()
```

```{python}
#| label: fig-qb-rushing
#| fig-cap: "Quarterbacks' share of their teams' rushing yards, 2006-2025: every run by a team's quarterbacks (players with 150 or more pass attempts that season), including designed runs, scrambles and sneaks, as a share of all rushing yards, league-wide, in the regular season. The 2012 read-option wave (shaded) shows as a step up; the Lamar Jackson era is a second, larger step, and in 2024 quarterbacks gained about one rushing yard in six. The numbers above the bars count quarterbacks who ran for 400 yards or more. Source: nflverse play-by-play."
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6.6, 3.0))
ax.axvspan(2011.5, 2013.5, color=style.LINE_TO_GAIN, alpha=0.15, lw=0)
cols = [style.OFFENSE if yr >= 2018 else style.MUTED for yr in QB_SHARE.index]
ax.bar(QB_SHARE.index, QB_SHARE.values, color=cols, width=0.72, zorder=2)
for yr, v in QB_SHARE.items():
    ax.text(yr, v + 0.35, f"{int(QB400.get(yr, 0))}", ha="center", fontsize=6.3, color=style.INK_2)
ax.text(2012.5, 18.6, "read-option\nwave", ha="center", fontsize=6.8, color=style.INK_2, va="top")
ax.annotate("Jackson's 1,206\nyards (2019)", xy=(2019, QB_SHARE.loc[2019] + 1.3), xytext=(2016.2, 17.6),
            fontsize=6.8, color=style.INK, ha="center", va="top",
            arrowprops=dict(arrowstyle="-", color=style.INK_2, lw=0.6))
ax.set_title("Numbers above the bars: quarterbacks who ran for 400+ yards that season", fontsize=7.5,
             loc="left", color=style.INK_2, fontweight="normal")
ax.set_xlim(2005.4, 2025.6)
ax.set_ylim(0, 19)
ax.set_xticks(range(2006, 2026, 2))
ax.tick_params(labelsize=7)
ax.set_ylabel("QB share of rushing yards (%)", fontsize=7.5)
ax.grid(axis="x", visible=False)
plt.show()
```

The chart makes two points.[^qbshare] First, quarterbacks went from about 7 percent of their teams'
rushing yards in the late 2000s to about 14 to 16 percent in 2020-2025, and the number of quarterbacks
running for 400 yards in a season roughly tripled. Second, and less obviously, the rise is not a spike
and fall like 2012. It is a plateau. Designed quarterback runs, the planned keeps in the read-option
chart of the last chapter, actually peaked league-wide around 2020-2022 and drifted down after; what
stayed is the quarterback as a runner of every kind: scrambling when the coverage is good, sneaking on
third-and-1, keeping on the read when the edge chases. A running quarterback stopped being a scheme and
became a skill that most good offenses expect their quarterback to have.

Why did it stick this time, when the 2012 wave faded in two seasons?

- **The arithmetic got better for it.** A quarterback who is a real running threat is an extra
  blocker's worth of math, the "plus one" of [Option Football](../03-the-run-game/03-04-option-football.qmd):
  the defense has to account for him, so one defender who would otherwise chase the back has to stay
  home. Against a two-high defense with six in the box, that turns six-against-six into a numbers
  advantage without changing personnel. The two-high counterrevolution made the running quarterback
  more valuable, not less.
- **The quarterbacks were built for it, and the offenses were built around them.** The 2012 wave
  grafted college plays onto NFL offenses for a season. Jackson's Ravens, Hurts's Eagles and Allen's
  Bills designed their whole run game, protection rules and passing game around a quarterback who ran,
  and drafted and paid him to be that player for a decade.
- **They learned to run like quarterbacks.** The modern running quarterback slides, gets out of bounds,
  and picks his moments; a large share of his yards come on scrambles, when the defense is in coverage
  and nobody is waiting to hit him. The read-option quarterbacks of 2012 took far more hits for every
  yard.
- **The short-yardage sneak became nearly automatic.** The tush push turned the quarterback's legs into
  the league's most reliable fourth-and-1 play. The league voted on banning it in May 2025: the
  proposal failed 22 to 10, two votes short. In 2026 no team even proposed a ban.[^tush]

::: {.callout-note title="Film room: Ravens 2019 — an offense designed for a runner"}
The 2019 Ravens went 14-2 and led the league in points. Watch them for what the opponents had to do.
Every running play has two possible ball carriers, so the edge defender on the side away from the back
can't chase him; he has to stay home for Jackson. Every play-action pass carries the threat that Jackson
will run it himself, so the defense's last line, the safeties, have to think about the run longer than
they want to. The Ravens added to the problem with personnel: they used two tight ends, and often a
fullback and three tight ends, far more than the league did.

**What to notice:** count the defenders who are watching Jackson rather than the back at the mesh, the
moment the ball is in both their hands. If it's one, the Ravens have the numbers somewhere else. The full
case study is [The Ravens' Option Run Game](../12-case-studies/12-05-ravens-lamar-run-game.qmd), which
treats 2019-2025 as a closed era: John Harbaugh was fired in January 2026 and is now the Giants' head
coach.
:::

## The coaches start trusting the math

The last chapter ended with an argument: David Romer's 2006 paper and Brian Burke's public models said
coaches kicked on fourth down far too often, and coaches mostly ignored them. In this era they stopped
ignoring them, and you can watch the moment it happened.

```{python}
#| code-summary: "Show the Python (fourth-down go rates, 2000-2025)"
#| output: false
_g = pbp(range(2000, 2026), columns=["season", "season_type", "down", "ydstogo", "play_type", "yardline_100",
                                      "wp", "half_seconds_remaining"])
_g = _g[(_g["season_type"] == "REG") & (_g["down"] == 4) & _g["play_type"].isin(["pass", "run", "punt", "field_goal"])
        & _g["wp"].between(0.2, 0.8) & (_g["half_seconds_remaining"] > 120)]
_g["go"] = _g["play_type"].isin(["pass", "run"])
GO = pd.DataFrame({
    "short_mid": _g[(_g["ydstogo"] <= 2) & _g["yardline_100"].between(30, 70)].groupby("season")["go"].mean(),
    "opp_short": _g[(_g["ydstogo"] <= 3) & (_g["yardline_100"] <= 50)].groupby("season")["go"].mean(),
    "all": _g.groupby("season")["go"].mean(),
}) * 100
```

```{python}
#| label: fig-fourth-down
#| fig-cap: "How often NFL teams went for it on fourth down, 2000-2025, in competitive situations (the offense's win probability between 20 and 80 percent, more than two minutes left in the half; a 'go' is a run or pass rather than a punt or field-goal try). Three cuts: fourth-and-1 or 2 between the 30-yard lines; fourth-and-3 or less in the opponent's half; and every fourth down. For eighteen seasons nothing moved, through Romer's paper (2006) and Belichick's famous fourth-and-2 (2009). From 2018 every line roughly doubles. Source: nflverse play-by-play."
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6.6, 3.3))
ax.axvspan(2017.5, 2025.5, color=style.OFFENSE_TINT, alpha=0.5, lw=0)
for col, lab, c in (("opp_short", "4th and 3 or less,\nopponent's half", style.SERIES[0]),
                    ("short_mid", "4th and 1-2,\nbetween the 30s", style.SERIES[1]),
                    ("all", "every 4th down", style.SERIES[2])):
    ax.plot(GO.index, GO[col], marker="o", ms=3.0, color=c, lw=1.8)
    ax.text(2025.5, GO.loc[2025, col], f" {GO.loc[2025, col]:.0f}%", fontsize=6.8, color=style.INK_2,
            va="center")
ax.text(2000.2, 45.0, "4th and 3 or less, opponent's half", fontsize=6.8,
        color=style.SERIES[0])
ax.text(2000.2, GO.loc[2000, "short_mid"] - 6.5, "4th and 1-2, between the 30s", fontsize=6.8,
        color="#b84a1f")
ax.text(2000.2, GO.loc[2000, "all"] + 3.0, "every fourth down", fontsize=6.8, color="#12805a")
for yr, txt, y in ((2006, "Romer's\npaper", 60), (2009, "Belichick's\n4th-and-2", 60)):
    ax.axvline(yr, color=style.MUTED, lw=0.7, ls=(0, (2, 2)))
    ax.text(yr, y, txt, fontsize=6.4, color=style.INK_2, ha="center", va="bottom",
            bbox=dict(boxstyle="round,pad=0.15", fc=style.SURFACE, ec="none"))
ax.text(2021.5, 84, "2018 on", fontsize=7, color=style.OFFENSE_DARK, ha="center")
ax.set_xlim(1999.5, 2027.3)
ax.set_ylim(0, 90)
ax.set_xticks(range(2000, 2026, 5))
ax.tick_params(labelsize=7)
ax.set_ylabel("went for it (%)", fontsize=7.5)
ax.grid(axis="x", visible=False)
plt.show()
```

The flat stretch is the striking part.[^gocalc] From 2000 to 2017, on fourth-and-1 or 2 between the 30s
in a close game, teams went for it about a quarter of the time, in almost every season. Romer's paper
didn't move it; Belichick's 2009 decision, and the uproar after it, didn't move it. Then, in five
seasons, the rate doubled, and by 2025 teams went on about 64 percent of those downs and on about
three-quarters of short fourth downs in the opponent's half. Why then?

- **The models went public, and onto the broadcast.** Ben Baldwin and Sebastian Carl's nflfastR, released
  in 2020, put expected points and win probability for every play since 1999 in anyone's hands, free
  (it is the ancestor of the nflverse data behind every chart in this book). Fourth-down calculators
