  appeared on websites (Baldwin's own, built on nflfastR, in 2020) and then on broadcasts (the NFL's
  Next Gen Stats Decision Guide, made for broadcasters, from the 2021 season), and a coach who punted on
  fourth-and-1 at midfield heard about it the next morning from people with numbers.[^fourthtools]
- **Teams hired analysts, and listened to them.** By the early 2020s nearly every team had an
  analytics staff, and several head coaches talked openly about using a fourth-down chart on game day.
- **A champion did it on the biggest stage.** Doug Pederson's 2017 Eagles were among the most aggressive
  teams in the league on fourth down, and on fourth-and-goal from the 1 at the end of the first half of
  Super Bowl LII they ran the "Philly Special," a direct snap to the running back, a pitch to the tight
  end and a touchdown pass to the quarterback, Nick Foles. They beat New England 41-33.[^philly]
- **New coaches with new habits.** The next wave of head coaches (Brandon Staley's 2021 Chargers, Dan
  Campbell's Lions, Nick Sirianni's Eagles) went for it constantly. In competitive situations, by this
  book's count, Campbell's Lions went for it more than any other team in 2021, 2022 and 2023.

::: {.callout-note title="Film room: Lions at 49ers, NFC Championship Game, January 28, 2024"}
The decision that tested the new orthodoxy. Detroit led San Francisco 24-7 at halftime. Early in the third
quarter, leading 24-10, the Lions faced fourth-and-2 at the 49ers' 28, inside field-goal range, and went
for it; Jared Goff's pass fell incomplete. Late in the fourth quarter, now trailing 27-24, they faced
fourth-and-3 at the 49ers' 30, where a field goal would have tied the game, and went for it again;
another incompletion. San Francisco won 34-31.[^nfccg]

**What to notice:** the same thing 2009's fourth-and-2 taught. Both decisions were judged by their
outcomes the next morning, and both were defensible on the numbers. ESPN's model called each one a toss-up
that leaned, by a fraction of a point, toward going for it (a 90.5 percent chance to win against 90.3 for
the field goal on the first; 39.1 against 38.8 on the second), and Next Gen Stats leaned the same way on
both, by one and two and a half points. No public model treated going for it as the reckless choice it was called.[^lionsmodels] What the night really showed
is how much the culture had changed: in 2009 Belichick's go was a scandal because coaches didn't do
that. In 2024 Campbell's were a scandal because they failed. Nobody argued that a coach shouldn't go
for it on fourth-and-2 at the opponent's 28; they argued about this one. Build the model yourself in
[Win Probability and Fourth Downs](../13-analytics-and-data/13-03-win-probability-and-fourth-down.qmd).
:::

Aggression spread beyond fourth down. Teams passed more on early downs than the situation predicted
([Tendencies, PROE, and Charting](../13-analytics-and-data/13-04-tendencies-proe-and-charting.qmd)
measures that), went for two more often, and used the new overtime rules
([Clock and Game Management](../10-situational-football/10-04-clock-and-game-management.qmd)) to plan
whole possessions around a coin flip. The common thread is the [go-for-it decision](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-go-for-it-decision)'s
logic: a decision is right or wrong before the snap, on its probabilities, not after it, on its result.

## The rules underneath, 2017-2026

The rules kept moving too. Most of the era's changes were about safety, and some of those changed
strategy more than any scheme did. One table, with the chapter that owns each rule:[^rules]

| Season | Rule | What it changed |
|--|------------|----------|
| 2017 | Regular-season overtime cut from 15 to 10 minutes | More ties possible; the first possession matters more ([Clock and Game Management](../10-situational-football/10-04-clock-and-game-management.qmd)) |
| 2018 | [Use of the helmet](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-use-of-the-helmet-2018-rule): lowering the head to initiate contact with the helmet is a foul, for any player | Tackling technique: defenders taught to tackle with the shoulder and head up ([Contact Rules and Penalties](../09-special-teams-and-the-rules-that-shape-strategy/09-03-contact-rules-and-penalties.qmd)) |
| 2018 | Kickoff alignment rules (no running start; five players on each side of the kicker) | The first of many kickoff redesigns ([Kickoffs and Returns](../09-special-teams-and-the-rules-that-shape-strategy/09-02-kickoffs-and-returns.qmd)) |
| 2019 | Pass interference reviewable by replay, for one season only | After the Rams-Saints NFC Championship no-call; almost never overturned, then dropped |
| 2022 | Playoff overtime: both teams get a possession | After the Bills-Chiefs "13 seconds" game; changes two-point and kick-or-receive math |
| 2024 | The [dynamic kickoff](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-dynamic-kickoff) (a one-year trial); [hip-drop tackle](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-hip-drop-tackle) banned; a third challenge if one of the first two succeeds | Kickoff returns come back; a tackling technique outlawed |
| 2025 | Dynamic kickoff made permanent, touchback to the 35; regular-season overtime gives both teams a possession; [replay assist](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-replay-assist) can correct some fouls; tush-push ban fails 22-10 | Kickoff returns on about three-quarters of kicks; field position shifts toward the offense |
| 2026 | Onside kick may be declared at any time, even when leading; a kickoff from the 50 that goes out of bounds is a touchback at the 20; a fourth "floater" in the receiving team's setup zone; replay officials may be consulted on ejections | Changed after the 2025 season: the newest kickoff tweaks ([Kickoffs and Returns](../09-special-teams-and-the-rules-that-shape-strategy/09-02-kickoffs-and-returns.qmd)) |

Two patterns in the table matter for how you watch. First, **kickoffs changed more than any other part
of the game**: five rule changes in nine seasons (2018, 2023, 2024, 2025 and 2026), and by 2025 a kickoff was returned about three times out
of four, where in 2023 it was returned about one time in five. Starting field position, and so the
fourth-down and two-minute math, moved with it. Second, **the league kept protecting the passing game
indirectly.** The helmet rule, the hip-drop ban and replay assist are safety rules, but every one of them
makes defenders a little more careful, and the 2022 and 2025 overtime changes reward offenses that can
score touchdowns, not field goals. Nothing in nine seasons tilted the field back toward defense; the
defenses had to do that with scheme.

## Where the game stands entering 2026

Which brings us back to Seattle.

::: {.callout-note title="Film room: Seahawks 2025 — the whole era on one team"}
Mike Macdonald built his reputation as the Ravens' defensive coordinator in 2022 and 2023, when Baltimore
allowed the fewest points in the league and led it in sacks. His defenses start from two-high shells and
then disguise everything after: safeties rotating at the snap,
[simulated pressures](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-simulated-pressure) that show six rushers and
send four ([Zone Blitz, Fire Zones, and Simulated Pressure](../07-pressure/07-03-zone-blitz-and-simulated-pressure.qmd)),
and linebackers standing in the A gaps before the snap. He became Seattle's head coach in 2024.[^macdonald]

In 2025 he hired Klint Kubiak, Gary Kubiak's son and a Shanahan-tree coach, as offensive coordinator, and
the Seahawks played the other half of this chapter: under center on 53 percent of their snaps, fewer than
three wide receivers on 55 percent, a fullback on the field more than most teams, outside zone and
play-action. They went 14-3, allowed the fewest points in the league, and beat New England 29-13 in
Super Bowl LX, with Jason Myers kicking a Super Bowl-record five field goals, Uchenna Nwosu returning an
interception for a touchdown, and Walker running for 135 yards. The defense played two-high on about 52
percent of opponents' dropbacks, the third-highest rate in the league, and still sacked Drake Maye six
times.[^seahawks25]

**What to notice:** that the same team is the era's answer on both sides. On defense, a two-high shell
that hides pressure, so the light box isn't a gift. On offense, a heavy, under-center run game built to
beat exactly that kind of defense. When you watch the 2026 Seahawks, watch whether the offense keeps its
shape without the coordinator who built it: Kubiak left after one season to become the Raiders' head coach,
and Brian Fleury, from Shanahan's staff, replaced him.
:::

The coaching map that Seattle sits on is changing fast. Kubiak to Las Vegas; Mike McDaniel, fired in
Miami, now the Chargers' offensive coordinator; Mike LaFleur, McVay's 2025 coordinator, now Arizona's
head coach; John Harbaugh in New York; a fourth straight new offensive coordinator in Philadelphia.
The Shanahan tree, which in 2025 supplied play-callers all over the league, is scattering into new
branches, and the 2026 staffs are not the 2025 ones.[^staffs26] Label every staff with its season when
you read about these teams.

And the rules enter 2026 changed again: onside kicks any time, a kick from the 50 out of bounds now a
touchback at the 20, a fourth floater in the return team's setup, replay allowed to advise on ejections,
the tush push still legal, and no 18-game season yet.[^rules26]

## The pattern: an arms race you can watch

Step back and the nine seasons make a loop, the same rhythm the last chapter found, only faster.

```{python}
#| label: fig-arms-race
#| fig-cap: "The arms race of 2010-2025 as a loop. Each box is a move; each arrow is the answer it provoked. Start at the top: Seattle's single-high defense put an eighth man in the box; McVay and Shanahan's play-action punished him; Mahomes punished anyone left alone deep; two-high defenses took away both and emptied the box; offenses answered with heavier personnel, the quarterback run and the snap from under center; and defenses answered that with base and big-nickel packages and pressure disguised inside a two-high shell. The dashed arrow is the open question entering 2026: what beats that?"
NODES = [
    ("2013-2016", "Single-high,\neighth man in the box", "Seattle's Cover 3", "def"),
    ("2017-2019", "One look: 11 personnel,\nmotion, play-action", "McVay, Shanahan", "off"),
    ("2018-2022", "Off-script and\nexplosive passing", "Mahomes, Reid", "off"),
    ("2019-2025", "Two-high shells,\nlight boxes, late rotation", "Fangio, Staley", "def"),
    ("2023-2025", "Heavy personnel, under\ncenter, the QB run", "Ravens, Eagles, Lions,\nRams, Seahawks", "off"),
    ("2024-2025", "Base and big nickel;\npressure from two-high", "Macdonald", "def"),
]
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6.6, 5.6))
ax.set_xlim(-1.62, 1.62)
ax.set_ylim(-1.32, 1.32)
ax.set_aspect("equal")
ax.axis("off")
n = len(NODES)
ang = [np.pi / 2 - i * 2 * np.pi / n for i in range(n)]
R = 1.0
pts = [(R * np.cos(t) * 1.18, R * np.sin(t)) for t in ang]
for i in range(n):
    x0, y0 = pts[i]
    x1, y1 = pts[(i + 1) % n]
    last = i == n - 1
    ax.add_patch(FancyArrowPatch((x0, y0), (x1, y1), connectionstyle="arc3,rad=-0.28", arrowstyle="-|>",
                                 mutation_scale=13, color=style.INK_2 if not last else style.MUTED,
                                 lw=1.3, ls="-" if not last else (0, (3, 2)), shrinkA=46, shrinkB=46, zorder=1))
for (x, y), (yrs, what, who, side) in zip(pts, NODES):
    ec, fc = (style.OFFENSE, style.OFFENSE_TINT) if side == "off" else (style.DEFENSE, style.DEFENSE_TINT)
    ax.text(x, y, f"{yrs}\n{what}\n({who})", ha="center", va="center", fontsize=7.2, color=style.INK,
            linespacing=1.2, zorder=3, bbox=dict(boxstyle="round,pad=0.45", fc=fc, ec=ec, lw=1.1))
ax.text(0, 0.06, "every answer\nbecomes the\nnext problem", ha="center", va="center", fontsize=9,
        color=style.INK_2, linespacing=1.3)
ax.text(0, -0.36, "2026: ?", ha="center", va="center", fontsize=10, color=style.INK, fontweight="bold")
ax.legend(handles=[
    Line2D([], [], marker="s", ls="", ms=9, markerfacecolor=style.OFFENSE_TINT, markeredgecolor=style.OFFENSE,
           label="offensive move"),
    Line2D([], [], marker="s", ls="", ms=9, markerfacecolor=style.DEFENSE_TINT, markeredgecolor=style.DEFENSE,
           label="defensive move")], loc="lower center", bbox_to_anchor=(0.5, -0.04), ncol=2, fontsize=7.5,
          frameon=False)
plt.show()
```

The loop is the best single tool this chapter can give you, because it tells you what to look for next.
Each box was a sensible answer to the box before it, and each one created a weakness the next box
attacked. The defense of 2025 (two-high, but with base personnel and disguised pressure ready for heavy
offenses) is an answer to heavy offenses. So the obvious question for 2026 is the one the last chapter
already asked: what does a heavy offense do when the defense matches it with big players? It spreads
them out. A team that lines up in 12 personnel against a base defense and then splits its tight ends
wide is asking a linebacker to cover a receiver, the Patriots' dilemma of 2011, fourteen years later.
Whether that, or something nobody has thought of, is the next arrow is what the 2026 season will
tell you.

| The move | The answer | What it opened up |
|--------|---------|--------|
| Single-high, eighth man in the box (Seattle) | McVay-Shanahan: one look, motion, play-action into the middle | Defenses needed to stop committing to the run before the snap |
| Off-script, explosive passing (Mahomes) | Keep everything in front: more two-high | Light boxes |
| Two-high, light boxes (Fangio, Staley) | Light-box run game: heavy personnel, under center, the running quarterback | Safeties forced to fit the run, and play-action behind them |
| Heavy personnel and the QB run | Base and big nickel; pressure disguised in a two-high shell (Macdonald) | Big defenders who can be spread out and isolated |
| Kicking on fourth down | Going for it, on the models' advice | Every fourth-and-short is now a play-call |

::: {.callout-tip title="Watch for it on Sunday: arms-race spotting"}
Pick one game and find one link of the loop in it: one offensive trend, and the defensive counter you
can see against it.

- **Before the first snap, set your baseline.** What personnel does the offense open with, and is the
  quarterback under center or in the shotgun? Count the deep safeties: one or two?
- **On first and second down, count the box.** Six or fewer with two safeties deep is a two-high, light-box
  defense. Is the offense running into it, and is the run getting five yards?
- **If the run is working, watch the safeties.** Does one start walking down before the snap, or
  sprinting down at the snap? That is the defense giving up its shell. Now watch for play-action behind
  him.
- **Count the tight ends and backs.** Two tight ends or a fullback on first down is the heavy answer.
  Does the defense match with a third linebacker or a third safety? If it does, does the offense then
  split a tight end out wide against a linebacker?
- **Watch the quarterback when the pocket breaks.** Does he run, and does the defense have a spy or a
  rusher who stays home for him?
- **On fourth-and-short in the opponent's half, predict before the coach decides.** In 2025 teams went
  for it about three times in four in that situation. Did this coach?
- **By halftime, name the link.** "The offense is running heavy into two-high boxes, and the defense
  just started rotating a safety down" is one. Write it down and see whether it changes in the second
  half.
:::

## Predict the play

::: {.callout-tip title="Predict the play 1: the safety who keeps creeping down (2019)"}
```{python}
#| label: fig-predict-creep
#| fig-cap: "2019, first-and-10 at midfield. A Shanahan-style offense in 21 personnel (fullback F and tight end Y, gold rings) under center; the receivers are in tight splits. It has run outside zone to the right three times this quarter for 5, 7 and 6 yards. The defense is single-high, and the strong safety (SS, ringed) has crept down to 5 yards, outside the tight end: eight defenders are in the box. The two linebackers are at 4.5 yards, eyes on the backfield."
off = line5() + [O("QB", "QB", -1.9, 0, "Q"), O("FB", "FB", -4.5, 1.2, "F"), O("RB", "RB", -7.0, 0.0, "R"),
                 O("Y", "TE", -0.7, 4.8, "Y"), O("X", "WR", -0.7, -10.5, "X"), O("Z", "WR", -1.5, 9.5, "Z")]
dfn = [D("WDE", "DE", 1.0, -4.4, "E"), D("WDT", "DT", 1.0, -0.7, "T"), D("SDT", "DT", 1.0, 2.35, "T"),
       D("SDE", "DE", 1.0, 5.6, "E"), D("WILL", "WILL", 4.5, -2.4), D("MIKE", "MIKE", 4.5, 1.8),
       D("SAM", "SAM", 3.5, 7.4), D("SS", "SS", 5.0, 9.6), D("LCB", "CB", 6.0, -11.0, "CB"),
       D("RCB", "CB", 6.5, 12.0, "CB"), D("FS", "FS", 13.5, -1.0)]
pr1 = Play(off, dfn, los=50, to_go=10)
pr1.highlight("FB", "Y", color=TE_RING)
pr1.highlight("SS", color=style.DEFENSE)
f = pr1.draw(lateral=(-17.0, 17.0), window=(-9.0, 17.0))
no_numbers(f.ax)
say(f, pr1, "one deep safety", (15.4, -1.0), fs=6.8)
pointer(f, pr1, "crept down\nto 5 yards", (9.6, 12.4), (5.6, 9.8), fs=6.6)
plt.show()
```

**The offense shows the same look a fourth time. What's the call, and where does the ball go?**

::: {.callout-tip title="Answer" collapse="true"}
**The play-action pass off the same outside-zone look, and the ball goes where the creeping safety and
the linebackers used to be.** Three straight runs of 5 or more yards are what made the safety creep
down; he is now a ninth run defender, and the defense has one deep safety for the whole field. Show the
fourth outside zone (the line steps right, the back and fullback run the same path), and the linebackers
and the strong safety will step toward it, because the last three times they were right to.

The most likely call in this offense is a boot away from the fake: the quarterback fakes right and
rolls left, the fullback slides into the left flat, X runs a vertical to take the left corner deep, and
Z, from the right, runs the deep crossing route across the field behind the linebackers, as in the
play-action figure earlier in the chapter. Against a defense this committed, the tight end leaking up
the seam behind the strong safety is the shot. Whatever the route, the principle is the McVay-Shanahan
one: the run earned the pass.

And notice what this picture taught defenses. A coordinator who keeps losing this play has two answers:
stop putting the eighth and ninth men near the line before the snap, or put them there and bring them
back at the snap. Both lead to two-high.
:::
:::

::: {.callout-tip title="Predict the play 2: second-and-6 against two-high (2022)"}
```{python}
#| label: fig-predict-twohigh
#| fig-cap: "2022, second-and-6. 11 personnel in the shotgun, tight end (Y, gold ring) attached on the right, a 2x2 receiver set. The defense is in nickel with both safeties (ringed) 12 to 13 yards deep: four linemen and two linebackers in the box (dashed rectangle), the nickel back ($) out over the slot receiver, both corners off."
off = line5() + [O("QB", "QB", -5.0, 0, "Q"), O("RB", "RB", -5.0, -1.6, "R"), O("Y", "TE", -0.7, 4.8, "Y"),
                 O("X", "WR", -0.7, -15.0, "X"), O("H", "WR", -1.5, -9.0, "H"), O("Z", "WR", -1.5, 14.0, "Z")]
dfn = [D("WDE", "DE", 1.0, -4.1, "E"), D("WDT", "DT", 1.0, -0.7, "T"), D("SDT", "DT", 1.0, 2.35, "T"),
       D("SDE", "DE", 1.0, 5.7, "E"), D("WILL", "WILL", 4.5, -2.0), D("MIKE", "MIKE", 4.5, 1.8),
       D("NB", "NB", 5.0, -9.6, "$"), D("LCB", "CB", 7.0, -15.0, "CB"), D("RCB", "CB", 7.0, 14.0, "CB"),
       D("FS", "FS", 12.5, -8.5), D("SS", "SS", 13.0, 8.5)]
pr2 = Play(off, dfn, los=45, to_go=6)
pr2.highlight("Y", color=TE_RING)
pr2.highlight("FS", "SS", color=style.DEFENSE)
f = pr2.draw(lateral=(-18.0, 18.0), window=(-8.5, 17.0))
no_numbers(f.ax)
box_outline(f, pr2, w=(-7.6, 7.6), d=(0.0, 6.6))
say(f, pr2, "6 in the box", (8.2, -3.0), fs=6.8, color=style.DEFENSE_DARK)
plt.show()
```

**Count the box and the blockers. Run or pass, and why is the defense comfortable with your answer?**

::: {.callout-tip title="Answer" collapse="true"}
**Run.** The box has six defenders (four linemen, two linebackers) and the offense has six blockers in
front of the back (five linemen and the attached tight end). Every box defender has a man, and the two
safeties are at 12 and 13 yards, so a run that gets through the line has five or six yards before anyone
can arrive. On second-and-6 that is a first down or a third-and-short. Inside zone or duo straight at
the box is the call; a quarterback who is a running threat makes it better still, because a read on the
backside end turns six-on-six into a numbers advantage.

**Why is the defense comfortable?** Because this is the trade it chose. A five-yard run here is worth a
little less than nothing to the offense on average (runs against light boxes in this era averaged about
−0.04 EPA), and the defense has kept both safeties over the top of every receiver, so the play that
would really hurt it, the 25-yard completion, is much harder. It is also not as static as it looks: one
of those safeties may be rotating down at the snap, which turns your "light box" into seven and your run
into a three-yard gain. That is why the offenses of 2023-2025 stopped settling for six-on-six and added a
seventh blocker.
:::
:::

::: {.callout-tip title="Predict the play 3: heavy personnel, no huddle (2025)"}
```{python}
#| label: fig-predict-heavy
#| fig-cap: "2025, first-and-10. On the previous play the offense used three receivers and the defense matched with nickel. Now, without huddling, the offense has lined up in 12 personnel (two tight ends, gold rings) with the quarterback under center, and the defense, unable to substitute, is still in nickel with two safeties deep. The strong safety (SS, ringed) is the defender whose job, in a light box, is to come down and fit the run."
off = line5() + [O("QB", "QB", -1.9, 0, "Q"), O("RB", "RB", -7.0, 0.0, "R"), O("Y", "TE", -0.7, 4.8, "Y"),
                 O("U", "TE", -1.6, 7.3, "U"), O("X", "WR", -0.7, -13.5, "X"), O("Z", "WR", -1.5, 12.0, "Z")]
dfn = [D("WDE", "DE", 1.0, -4.4, "E"), D("WDT", "DT", 1.0, -0.7, "T"), D("SDT", "DT", 1.0, 2.35, "T"),
       D("SDE", "DE", 1.0, 5.9, "E"), D("WILL", "WILL", 4.5, -1.8), D("MIKE", "MIKE", 4.5, 2.6),
       D("NB", "NB", 5.0, -9.0, "$"), D("LCB", "CB", 7.0, -13.5, "CB"), D("RCB", "CB", 7.0, 12.0, "CB"),
       D("FS", "FS", 12.5, -7.5), D("SS", "SS", 12.5, 7.5)]
pr3 = Play(off, dfn, los=35, to_go=10)
pr3.highlight("Y", "U", color=TE_RING)
pr3.highlight("SS", color=style.DEFENSE)
f = pr3.draw(lateral=(-17.0, 17.0), window=(-9.0, 17.0))
no_numbers(f.ax)
box_outline(f, pr3, w=(-8.3, 8.3), d=(0.0, 7.3))
say(f, pr3, "6 in the box", (8.6, -2.6), fs=6.8, color=style.DEFENSE_DARK)
say(f, pr3, "7 blockers", (-4.0, -8.8), fs=6.8, color=style.OFFENSE_DARK)
plt.show()
```

**You're the defensive coordinator, and you can't substitute. What are your options on this snap, and
which one is the offense hoping you pick?**

::: {.callout-tip title="Answer" collapse="true"}
You have three options, and the offense has a play for each.

- **Stay in two-high with six in the box.** The offense has seven blockers (five linemen and two tight
  ends, both on the right) against your six box defenders, plus a back. That is an outside-zone run to the
  tight ends' side, and your nickel back ($) is on the far side of the field. Expect five yards or more.
- **Rotate the strong safety down at the snap** to make it seven against seven. Now you're single-high,
  and the strong safety is fitting a run that may be a fake: this is the play-action figure of the under-center
  section, the post or the deep over behind the safety who came down. The offense is under center
  precisely so that its run and its fake look the same to him.
- **Slant and stunt the front, or bring pressure from the two-high shell**, the Macdonald answer:
  move your linemen at the snap so the blocking angles are wrong, or send a linebacker into the gap the
  extra blocker was meant for while the safeties stay home. This is a guess, and against the right call
  it wins big; against the wrong one, the run goes for a lot.

**Which does the offense want?** Usually the second. The heavy, under-center offense is designed to make
the run good enough that the safety must come, and then to throw behind him; that is where its big plays
are. That is also why, after this snap, the defense will try very hard to get a base package or a third
safety on the field the next time those two tight ends come in, and why the offense will then try to
split them out wide against linebackers. The 2025 rise in base defense, from 20.5 percent of snaps in
2023 to 29.7 percent, is that next move.
:::
:::

## Takeaways

- **McVay and Shanahan won 2017-2019 with sameness.** One personnel group, tight splits, motion, and
  play-action off the outside zone from under center made every play look like a run, and pulled the
  linebackers and the box safety of single-high defenses out of the intermediate middle.
- **Mahomes and Reid added what a defense can't scout:** a college-borrowed passing game and a
  quarterback whose best plays came after the design broke down. Together with McVay, they pushed
  defenses to keep more players deep.
- **The two-high counterrevolution** (Fangio, Staley, and their trees) kept two safeties deep, played the
  run with six in the box and safeties fitting late, and disguised its coverage until the snap. Two-high
  coverage rose from about a third of dropbacks in 2018 to a record 42 percent in 2025; the price was
  light boxes and four- to five-yard runs.
- **Offenses answered with the light-box run game and the under-center revival.** More blockers than the
  defense has box defenders (12 and 13 personnel, the fullback, the running quarterback), a run from under
  center that looks exactly like the play-action pass, and a deep safety forced to guess. In 2025 offenses
  used fewer than three receivers on about 42 percent of plays and went under center on about a third.
- **Positions mutated to fit the race**: the nickel became the base, the star and big nickel answered heavy
  sets, linebackers got lighter, the move tight end became the offense's hinge, the edge rusher became the
  premium defender, and the fullback found a niche. And the **quarterback run became normal**, because it
  adds a blocker's worth of math against a light box and because the quarterbacks were built and protected
  for it.
- **Coaches started trusting the math, and the rules kept moving.** Fourth-and-short go rates doubled
  after 2018; kickoffs, overtime and contact rules changed almost every year. Seattle's Super Bowl LX team,
  two-high on defense and heavy and under center on offense, is where the race stood entering 2026.

Fourth-and-1 or 2 between the 30s: 20-33 percent every season 2000-2017, 36 (2018), 52 (2020), 64 percent (2025). Fourth-and-3 or less in the opponent's half: 28 (2000), 38 (2017), 51 (2018), 75 percent (2025). All fourth downs: 6-9 percent 2000-2017, 18 percent in 2025. Most go-for-its in those situations: Detroit in 2021 (18), 2022 (20) and 2023 (19); the 2021 Chargers were second (17).

The NGS Decision Guide was announced by the NFL and AWS for the 2021 season, for broadcasters to show the go, kick and punt win probabilities: GeekWire (2021): https://www.geekwire.com/2021/punt-go-aws-latest-analytics-nfl-helps-fans-second-guess-4th-play-calls/ ; NFL.com, "Introducing the Next Gen Stats Decision Guide": https://www.nfl.com/news/introducing-the-next-gen-stats-decision-guide-a-new-analytics-tool-for-fourth-do .
